docs.title: Use of AI assistance
docs.text: LoopSage is not a product of AI generation. It is an idea that has evolved over all the years of my PhD, and the model, its design and its scientific choices are mine. The implementation, however, is mostly the work of one person, and the project grew large. I therefore used an AI assistant (an agent) to help write the documentation and to help with parts of the code, working under my direction and review.

docs.title: Software
docs.text: LoopSage builds on open-source software: OpenMM for molecular dynamics, numba and NumPy for the Monte Carlo sampler, hic-straw for reading Hi-C files, and MkDocs Material for this documentation. Thanks to their authors and maintainers.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
How LoopSage works inside: the flow of the program and, for each stage, what it does, which parameters control it and where the code is. The pages follow the order in which the stages run.

  • The Pipeline: the flow chart of LoopSage, the stages, how they hand their results to each other, how to run one stage alone and what the run folder contains.
  • Preprocessing: how BEDPE loops, CTCF peaks, BigWig tracks and Hi-C maps are read and modelled, and the two binding modes (preferential and contrastive).
  • The Motif Finder: how the orientation of CTCF sites is read from the DNA sequence of the loop anchors.
  • The Optimizer: the mathematics of the parameter search (loss, Nelder–Mead, early stopping) and how to use it.
  • Monte Carlo: the energy of LoopSage, the moves (rebinding, sliding, epigenetic changes) and all parameters of the sampler.
  • Molecular Dynamics: how a loop snapshot becomes a 3D structure: forces, the Langevin integrator and the simulation arguments.

docs.title: Molecular Dynamics
docs.text:
The Monte Carlo stage tells us which beads are held together by loops in each snapshot. It says nothing about where the beads are in space. The molecular dynamics (MD) stage turns each snapshot into a 3D structure: it builds a polymer, ties the loop anchors together with springs, and lets the chain relax and move. The set of structures of all snapshots is the 3D ensemble.

The stage uses OpenMM, a molecular simulation library. It is optional (--run-MD).

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Think of the chromatin fibre as a string of \(N\) beads. In each frame:

  1. the string is a chain of beads held by bonds, and it resists bending and passing through itself;
  2. the loops of the Monte Carlo snapshot are added as springs between the two anchor beads of each loop;
  3. the system is simulated for a number of MD steps, so the chain can find a shape that agrees with all springs;
  4. the final positions are saved, and the next frame starts from them with the loops of the next snapshot.

Step 4 matters. The simulation is not restarted for every frame. It continues from the previous structure, and only the springs are exchanged. Neighbouring snapshots have almost the same loops, so the structure changes gradually and a few thousand steps per frame are enough to relax it. The number of steps per frame, sim_step, is therefore the relaxation time between two sets of loops: a larger number gives the chain more time to adapt, a smaller one gives faster but more correlated structures.

Units

Lengths are in nanometres and energies in kJ/mol, but the model is coarse-grained: a bead is a few kb of chromatin and the bond length is 0.1 nm in the force field. The numbers are model units, not real nanometres of a nucleus, and the time of a frame is a model time, not a measured one. Only ratios, contact patterns and shapes are meant to be compared with data.

docs.title: The forces
docs.text:
The force field is a sum of simple terms. They are all potential energies: the simulation moves the beads to lower the total.

Force What it does Form Option Bonds keeps neighbouring beads at distance \(r_0=0.1\) nm \(\tfrac12 k\,(r-r_0)^2\), \(k=3\cdot10^{5}\) kJ/mol/nm² (fixed) Angles stiffness: penalises bending away from a straight line \(\tfrac12 k_\theta(\theta-\pi)^2\) angle_ff_strength Excluded volume beads repel when they come close, so the chain cannot pass through itself a soft power law, see below ev_ff_strength, ev_ff_power Loop springs pulls the two anchors of every loop together \(\tfrac12 k_L(r-r_L)^2\) le_ff_length (\(r_L\)), le_ff_strength (\(k_L\)) Compartments (optional) beads in the same epigenetic state attract each other a Gaussian well do_compartments, comp_strength, comp_range

Excluded volume. The repulsion between two beads at distance \(r\) is

\[ U_{\mathrm{ev}}(r)=\left(\frac{\varepsilon^2\,\sigma^2}{r+r_s}\right)^{p},\qquad \sigma^2=\texttt{ev\_ff\_strength},\ \ \varepsilon=0.05,\ \ r_s=0.1\ \mathrm{nm},\ \ p=\texttt{ev\_ff\_power}. \]

It is large when two beads overlap and decays quickly with distance; the exponent \(p\) decides how steep: a larger \(p\) gives a harder, shorter-ranged wall, and a smaller \(p\) a softer, longer-ranged one (the default is \(p=6\): a hard core at contact, but a weaker push at a distance than \(p=3\), so the chain is not over-avoiding; at the default strength the crossing barrier is about \(15\,k_BT\), against \(5\,k_BT\) for \(p=3\)). The softening \(r_s\) keeps the force finite when beads touch. How hard the wall must be is a real question: if it is too soft, two strands can pass through each other, which creates unphysical knots and links; see Topology, where the same force is used to set a barrier of a chosen height.

Loop springs. The springs are the only link between the Monte Carlo and the 3D structure. They are replaced in every frame: the old springs are removed and the springs of the new snapshot added. A stiff spring (\(k_L=6\cdot10^4\)) and a short rest length (\(r_L=0.1\) nm) mean that the two anchors of a loop are practically in contact.

Compartments. When the epigenetic model was on in the Monte Carlo (epi_coeff > 0) and you set do_compartments = True, every bead carries the state it had in the snapshot, and two beads in the same state attract each other,

\[ U_{\mathrm{comp}}(r)=s\,E_{ab}\,e^{-r^2/2w^2},\qquad w=\texttt{comp\_range}\cdot\sqrt N\ \mathrm{nm}. \]

\(E_{ab}\) is a small table: it is non-zero only for two beads of the same state, and it is largest for state 0 (B) and weaker for the others, so that B beads aggregate more strongly than A beads. The scale \(s\) is comp_strength: 1 is the full strength of the table, lower values give softer compartments that stay open instead of collapsing into one dense ball. The states are updated in every frame, so compartments follow the Monte Carlo.

docs.title: The integrator
docs.text:
An integrator is the rule that moves the beads from one time step to the next. LoopSage uses one: the Langevin integrator of OpenMM. It solves Newton's equation of motion for every bead, with two extra ingredients that mimic the surrounding fluid: a friction force that slows the bead down, and random kicks that keep it moving. Friction and kicks are tied together so that the chain reaches the temperature you set, and the structures it samples are those of a polymer in thermal equilibrium with the springs of the current loops.

There are no other integrators to choose from, but the Langevin integrator has three numbers that you set:

Option Default Meaning integrator_step (--step-size) 100 fs the time step: how far the dynamics advances in one iteration sim_temp (--temperature) 310 K the temperature of the heat bath; it sets the size of the random kicks friction 0.1 / ps how strongly the beads are slowed down; a larger value gives slower, more overdamped motion

A larger time step makes the simulation faster, but too large a step makes it unstable. If the coordinates become infinite the run stops with the message that the MD became unstable; the cure is a smaller --step-size, or softer forces (a smaller le_ff_strength or ev_ff_strength).

docs.title: The steps of the stage
docs.text:
Build. The initial chain is made in a chosen shape (initial_structure_type: rw random walk, confined_rw, self_avoiding_rw, circle, helix, spiral or sphere), the forces are added, and the energy is minimised once (the beads are moved downhill until the force is below tolerance), so that the first frame does not start from overlapping beads.

Platform. OpenMM can run on a GPU or on CPU cores. With platform = auto LoopSage tries CUDA, then OpenCL, then the CPU; if a platform is listed but cannot start (a driver problem), it moves on to the next one. On the CPU the number of threads is the --threads value (all cores if you gave none). device picks a GPU when there are several.

Frames. For every Monte Carlo snapshot (after the burn-in when md_skip_burnin is on, otherwise all of them): swap the loop springs and the compartment states, run sim_step integrator steps, then record the positions, the radius of gyration, the potential energy, the distance matrix and the contact map. Each structure is also written as a .cif file when save_ensemble is on.

The simulated time of one frame is sim_step \(\times\) integrator_step (with the defaults \(5000\times100\) fs \(=500\) ps). The default of 5000 steps per frame was chosen so that the chain relaxes between two sets of loops.

Contact maps. A contact map is built from the distances \(d_{ij}\) of every frame with a Gaussian kernel \(e^{-d_{ij}^2/2\rho^2}\), where \(\rho\) is contact_radius (default 1 nm), and averaged over the frames. Its comparison with Hi-C is part of the Analysis stage.

docs.title: Topoisomerase options
docs.text: Real chromatin is not a polymer that can never cross itself: topoisomerases let strands pass through each other. Two optional modes switch the excluded volume off for a short time, so that strands can cross (topo_mode = random with ev_p, or topo_mode = local with topo_rate, topo_radius, topo_width, topo_window, topo_keep). Whether the chain crosses itself without help can be counted with track_crossings. This is the subject of the Topology page.

docs.title: The arguments
docs.text:
[molecular_dynamics]
run_md       = True          # run this stage                                  (CLI: --run-MD)
platform     = auto          # auto, CUDA, OpenCL, CPU or Reference            (CLI: --platform)
device       =               # GPU index, empty = default

initial_structure_type = rw  # rw, confined_rw, self_avoiding_rw, circle, helix, spiral, sphere
                             #                                                 (CLI: --init-structure)
# integrator (Langevin)
integrator_step = 100.0      # time step, fs                                   (CLI: --step-size)
sim_step        = 5000       # MD steps per Monte Carlo snapshot (frame)       (CLI: --md-steps)
sim_temp        = 310.0      # temperature, K                                  (CLI: --temperature)
friction        = 0.1        # 1/ps
tolerance       = 0.001      # energy minimisation, kJ/mol/nm

# forces
angle_ff_strength = 50.0     # stiffness, kJ/mol/rad^2
ev_ff_strength    = 100.0    # excluded volume strength, kJ/mol
ev_ff_power       = 6.0      # excluded volume exponent
le_ff_length      = 0.1      # loop spring rest length, nm
le_ff_strength    = 60000.0  # loop spring constant, kJ/mol/nm^2

# compartments (needs epi_coeff > 0 in [energy])
do_compartments = False
comp_strength   = 0.25       # scale of the interaction table
comp_range      = 0.03       # range in units of sqrt(N) nm

md_skip_burnin  = False      # only use snapshots after the Monte Carlo burn-in
save_ensemble   = True       # write the structures (frames as .cif, trajectory)  (CLI: --save-ensemble)

[analysis]
contact_radius  = 1.0        # nm, for the MD contact maps

Typical changes

For a more flexible, more compact chain lower angle_ff_strength; for a stiffer, more extended one raise it. For stronger aggregation of A and B compartments raise comp_strength. To let the structure relax longer between two sets of loops raise --md-steps. To save time while testing, lower --md-steps and save fewer snapshots (a larger --sample-every).

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: The coordinates of all frames, the radius of gyration, the energies and the average contact and distance maps are saved in data/md.npz. The folder structures/ contains the initial structure (init_structure.cif), the trajectory (trajectory.dcd) and, with save_ensemble, one file MDLE_<k>.cif per frame in structures/ensemble/. The 3D stage then builds the interactive viewer and the videos from these frames.

docs.title: Monte Carlo
docs.text: The Monte Carlo stage is the heart of LoopSage. It answers one question: given the anchors in this region, which sets of loops are likely? It does not simulate real time. It draws many sets of loops (snapshots) at random, in such a way that sets with a low energy appear more often than sets with a high energy. The 3D structures are built later from these snapshots.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
The chromatin is a line of \(N\) beads. The state of the system is described by:

  • \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) loop extrusion factors (LEFs, the cohesin rings). Each one is a loop between two beads, a left leg \(m_i\) and a right leg \(n_i\) with \(m_i<n_i\). Loops may overlap and nest;
  • optionally, an epigenetic state \(S_k\in\{0,1,\dots\}\) for every bead (for example B, neutral, A), used to model compartments.

A state is probable when its energy \(E\) is low. At temperature \(T\) the probability of a state is proportional to \(e^{-E/T}\) (the Boltzmann distribution), and the Metropolis rule below produces exactly these probabilities. The temperature \(T\) is in arbitrary units; it only says how much noise is allowed: a high \(T\) accepts many unfavourable moves, a low \(T\) almost none.

docs.title: The energy
docs.text:
The total energy is a sum of terms, each with one coefficient that you can change:

\[ E = E_{\mathrm{fold}} + E_{\mathrm{bind}} + E_{\mathrm{cross}} \;(+\,E_{\mathrm{tracks}}) \;(+\,E_{\mathrm{epi}}). \]

The first three terms are always present; the extra tracks and the epigenetic term are optional and zero unless switched on.

We go through them one by one. In all formulas the sum over \(i\) runs over the LEFs.

docs.title: Folding: long loops are good
docs.text:
\[ E_{\mathrm{fold}} = f\,c_f\sum_i \ln(n_i-m_i),\qquad c_f=-\frac{N}{N_{\mathrm{lef}}\,\ln(N/N_{\mathrm{lef}})} . \]

The constant \(c_f\) is negative, so a longer loop has a lower energy: extruders want to grow. The logarithm makes the gain smaller and smaller for very long loops, so that nothing grows without bound, and the normalisation \(c_f\) makes the coefficient \(f\) (folding_coeff, default 1) comparable for different numbers of beads and extruders. A second family of extruders (n_lef2, for example a different kind of ring) has its own coefficient \(f_2\) (folding_coeff2).

docs.title: Binding: legs like anchors
docs.text:
\[ E_{\mathrm{bind}} = b\,c_b\sum_i \big(L_{m_i}+R_{n_i}\big),\qquad c_b=-\frac{2N}{N_{\mathrm{anchors}}}, \]

where \(L\) and \(R\) are the anchor profiles from Preprocessing and \(N_{\mathrm{anchors}}\) is the number of anchors in the input. Again \(c_b<0\): a left leg on a bead with a high \(L\) and a right leg on a bead with a high \(R\) lower the energy. The coefficient \(b\) is bind_coeff. Which profile is used (preferential or contrastive) is decided in the preprocessing, see Preferential and contrastive binding. In the 2D mode (data_loss_mode = 1) the term uses the loop map, \(E_{\mathrm{bind}}=b\,c_b\sum_i J^{\mathrm{loss}}_{m_i n_i}\), and scores the pair of legs.

Contrastive mode. With binding_mode = contrastive the binding term gets a second part that looks at the beads inside each loop:

\[ E_{\mathrm{bind}} = b\,c_b\sum_i\Big[\big(L_{m_i}+R_{n_i}\big)+\frac{1}{\bar\ell}\sum_{k=m_i}^{n_i-1}\hat c_k\Big], \]

where \(\hat c_k\in[-1,1]\) is the coverage score of bead \(k\) (−1 only where the input has no loops, 0 where it has some, up to +1 where it has many) (see Preprocessing) and \(\bar\ell\) is the mean input loop length, which keeps the second part on the scale of one anchor. Since \(c_b<0\), a loop is rewarded for spanning beads with \(\hat c>0\) and penalised for spanning loop-free beads (\(\hat c=-1\)). The inner sum is a difference of prefix sums, \(P_{n_i}-P_{m_i}\) with \(P_j=\sum_{k<j}\hat c_k\), so a move costs \(O(1)\). In preferential mode only the first part is used.

docs.title: Crossing: loops should not cross
docs.text:
\[ E_{\mathrm{cross}} = \kappa\,10^{4}\sum_{i<j}K_{ij}, \qquad K_{ij}=\begin{cases}1 & \text{if loops } i,j \text{ interleave } (m_i<m_j<n_i<n_j)\\ 1 & \text{if they share a leg position}\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases} \]

Two loops that cross, or that sit on the same bead, would be hard to build in 3D without the polymer passing through itself. The huge constant \(10^4\) makes this penalty act almost as a rule: the sampler practically never keeps such a state. Nested loops (one inside the other) and neighbouring loops are free. The coefficient is \(\kappa\) (cross_coeff).

cross_loop               = True    # penalise interleaved loops, not only shared legs
between_families_penalty = True    # count crossings between the two LEF families too

docs.title: Extra tracks
docs.text: Each BigWig track \(t\) adds a term \(r_t\sum_i (B^t_{m_i}+B^t_{n_i})/\sum_k B^t_k\), where \(B^t\) is the track and \(r_t\) its strength (bw_strengths). It works like the binding term, with a signal that is not a loop anchor.

docs.title: Epigenetic states (the Potts term)
docs.text:
When epi_coeff \(=\varepsilon>0\), every bead carries a state and the energy gets

\[ E_{\mathrm{epi}} = -\varepsilon\Big[\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\,\delta(S_i,S_j)\;+\;\sum_k h_k\,S_k\Big]. \]

This is a Potts model. The first sum rewards pairs of beads that are linked (\(J_{ij}=1\)) and in the same state (\(\delta=1\) when \(S_i=S_j\), otherwise 0). The links are the chain neighbours and the current loops, so beads that a loop brings together tend to share the same state, and compartments grow from loops. The second sum is an external field: \(h_k\) comes from the compartment track (see Compartments from Hi-C), so A beads (\(h>0\)) are pulled to the high states and B beads (\(h<0\)) to the low ones. With \(\varepsilon=0\) the term is off, which is the default and gives the pure loop-extrusion model.

epi_coeff       = 0.0        # 0 = off; > 0 turns on the epigenetic states
n_epi_states    = 3          # number of states (B, neutral, A)
epigenetic_mode = dynamic    # J follows the current loops (dynamic) or is fixed from the input (static)
p_epigenetic    = 0.5        # share of the steps that change a state instead of moving a LEF

docs.title: The moves
docs.text:
One Monte Carlo step consists of \(2N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) attempted moves, so on average every LEF is touched twice. Each attempt does the following:

  1. With probability p_epigenetic (only if the epigenetic model is on) it changes the state of one random bead. Otherwise it picks one LEF at random and tries one of two moves with equal chance:
  2. Rebinding. The LEF is removed and loaded again somewhere else as the smallest possible loop, \((m,m+2)\). The place is a random bead, or, if you give a loading track, chosen in proportion to that track.
  3. Sliding. The two legs move by one bead each, independently and in a random direction (a random walk), so the loop can grow or shrink. A leg that would land on another loop's leg stays where it was, and a loop is never shorter than two beads. With lef_rw = False the legs only move outward, which is pure extrusion.

The three moves. a A LEF unbinds and loads again as a minimal loop. b The legs slide. c One bead changes its epigenetic state (red = A, blue = B); with the dynamic coupling the beads linked by the chain and by loops count.

docs.title: Accept or reject
docs.text:
For every move the change of energy \(\Delta E\) is computed (only the terms that involve the moved LEF or bead are recomputed, so the cost does not grow with the number of loops). The move is then accepted with the Metropolis probability

\[ p_{\mathrm{accept}}=\min\!\big(1,\;e^{-\Delta E/T}\big). \]

A move that lowers the energy is always accepted. A move that raises it is accepted with a probability that falls with \(\Delta E\) and rises with \(T\). This is what lets the system escape from a bad arrangement while still preferring good ones.

docs.title: Temperature: Metropolis or annealing
docs.text: With method = Metropolis the temperature is constant, \(T=T_{\mathrm{init}}\). With method = Annealing (default) the temperature falls linearly from \(T_{\mathrm{init}}\) to \(T_{\mathrm{final}}\) over the run, so the system first explores freely and then settles. Because snapshots are saved all the time, early snapshots are hotter, and the first part is removed by the burn-in.

docs.title: LEF speeds
docs.text:
Sliding picks the LEF uniformly by default, so all LEFs are equally fast. With lef_speed_dist the LEFs get different speeds and the faster ones are chosen more often for sliding. The mean speed is always 1.

lef_speed_dist Speeds constant all equal maxwell Maxwell–Boltzmann: the speed of a particle with a Gaussian velocity in 3D lognormal \(\ln v\) is Gaussian with width lef_speed_spread two_state a fraction lef_fast_fraction of fast LEFs, lef_fast_ratio times faster than the others

docs.title: Snapshots and statistics
docs.text:
The stage runs n_steps steps and saves the loops of all LEFs (and all states) every mc_step steps. The first burnin steps are burn-in: the system is still forgetting its random start (and, with annealing, is hot), so these snapshots are kept but not used for statistics. The snapshots after the burn-in are the production ensemble, and with replicas > 1 several independent chains are run in parallel and pooled. For every snapshot the stage also records the energy terms (total, binding, crossing, folding) and the unfolded fraction, the share of the chain not covered by any loop.

Checking convergence

The report shows the energy terms after the burn-in with a drift: the difference between the two halves of the production run in units of the standard deviation. A drift well below 1 means that the energy is stable; a large drift means that the run is too short (raise n_steps) or the burn-in too small.

docs.title: The arguments
docs.text:
All options of this stage, grouped:

[monte_carlo]
n_steps    = 20000       # total Monte Carlo steps                       (CLI: --mc-steps)
mc_step    = 200         # one snapshot every this many steps            (CLI: --sample-every)
burnin     = 1000        # steps whose snapshots are not used            (CLI: --burnin)
method     = Annealing   # Metropolis or Annealing                       (CLI: --method)
t_init     = 3.0         # starting temperature (a.u.)                   (CLI: --t-init)
t_final    = 1.0         # final temperature, Annealing only             (CLI: --t-final)
n_lef      =             # extruders (empty: number of anchors / 2)      (CLI: --n-lef)
n_lef2     = 0           # a second family of extruders
lef_rw     = True        # legs slide as a random walk                   (CLI: --lef-rw)
lef_speed_dist = constant   # constant, maxwell, lognormal, two_state    (CLI: --lef-speed)
variable_sliding_step = False   # step uniform in [1, shortest input loop] beads
replicas   = 1           # independent chains, pooled                    (CLI: --n-replicas)

[energy]
folding_coeff  = 1.0     # f:     reward for long loops
bind_coeff     = 1.0     # b:     reward for legs on anchors
cross_coeff    = 1.0     # kappa: penalty for crossing loops
epi_coeff      = 0.0     # epsilon: epigenetic coupling, 0 = off

Which ones to tune

The numbers that decide the look of the result are \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\), \(f\), \(b\) and the temperature. The optimizer fits exactly these four to a target. The crossing coefficient \(\kappa\) is better left at 1: it is a constraint more than a preference. The number of steps only needs to be large enough for the energy to be stable.

docs.title: The Motif Finder
docs.text:
The direction of a CTCF site decides which legs of a ring it can stop (see Loop extrusion): a forward site stops a leg that moves left, a reverse site stops a leg that moves right. Loop files such as ChIA-PET or HiChIP tell us where the two anchors of a loop are, but not in which direction the CTCF sites point. The motif finder reads this direction from the DNA sequence. It searches each anchor of a loop for the CTCF motif on both strands, turns the hits into a probability that the site is reversed, and writes this probability into the loop file. The Monte Carlo stage then uses it to build the profiles \(L\) and \(R\).

It is an optional step: it runs when a reference genome is given (--motif-genome), and the plain BEDPE import keeps working without it.

docs.title: The mathematics
docs.text: The idea is simple. We slide a small window along the DNA, give every window a score that tells us how much it looks like a CTCF site, and keep the windows that score high. In this section we will see how the score is built, how high it has to be, and how the hits end up as one number per anchor. To keep things friendly, we follow a tiny made-up motif of length \(L=3\) all the way through, so you can check every formula by hand.

docs.title: From known sites to a score
docs.text:
Notation. DNA is a string written with four letters (bases) \(b\in\{A,C,G,T\}\). A motif is a short pattern of length \(L\) that a protein likes to bind; we number its positions \(i=1,\dots,L\). A window \(x=x_1x_2\dots x_L\) is a piece of DNA of the same length, which we want to compare with the motif.

Counts. We start from a collection of \(N\) DNA sites that are known to be bound by the protein. At every position we simply count how often each base appears: \(c_{b,i}\) is the number of sites with base \(b\) at position \(i\). This table is the position frequency matrix (PFM). In the toy example, with \(N=10\) sites:

\(i=1\) \(i=2\) \(i=3\) A 8 0 0 C 0 10 1 G 1 0 9 T 1 0 0

Reading the columns: position 1 is mostly A, position 2 is always C, and position 3 is mostly G, so the motif is roughly ACG. For CTCF the table has \(L=19\) columns (JASPAR MA0139.1).

Probabilities. The fraction \(c_{b,i}/N\) would be a natural probability of base \(b\) at position \(i\). There is a catch, though. A base that was never seen (say G at position 2) would get probability \(0\), and any window with a G there would be rejected for ever, even if it matches perfectly everywhere else. Absence in a small sample does not mean impossible, so we give every base a tiny benefit of the doubt, a pseudocount \(\alpha\) (motif_pseudocount, default \(0.8\)), shared equally among the four bases,

\[ p_{b,i}=\frac{c_{b,i}+\alpha/4}{N+\alpha}. \]

A quick check: the four numbers at one position still add up to 1, because the four shares \(\alpha/4\) add up to \(\alpha\). In the toy example, \(p_{A,1}=(8+0.2)/10.8=0.76\) and \(p_{G,2}=0.2/10.8=0.019\): unlikely, but not impossible.

Log-odds. How do we decide whether a window is motif-like? We compare two stories: the window was drawn from the motif, or it is random DNA, in which every base has probability \(1/4\) at every position. At one position the ratio of the two probabilities is \(p_{b,i}/(1/4)\). Windows have \(L\) independent positions, so the ratios multiply. Long products of small numbers are awkward, so we take the logarithm (base 2), which turns the product into an easy sum. The position weight matrix (PWM) is

\[ M_{b,i}=\log_2\frac{p_{b,i}}{1/4}, \]

and the score of a window is

\[ S(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{L}M_{x_i,\,i}=\log_2\prod_{i=1}^{L}\frac{p_{x_i,i}}{1/4}. \]

The right-hand form says what \(S\) means: \(2^{S}\) is how many times more likely the window is under the motif than under random DNA. So each point of score is one doubling. A base that is more common than \(1/4\) in the motif adds a positive number, and a base that is rarer takes points away.

In the toy example the matrix is

\(i=1\) \(i=2\) \(i=3\) A \(+1.60\) \(-3.75\) \(-3.75\) C \(-3.75\) \(+1.92\) \(-1.17\) G \(-1.17\) \(-3.75\) \(+1.77\) T \(-1.17\) \(-3.75\) \(-3.75\)

so the consensus window ACG scores \(1.60+1.92+1.77=5.29\) (it is \(2^{5.29}\approx 39\) times more likely under the motif than at random), the window TCG scores \(-1.17+1.92+1.77=2.52\), and ACT scores \(1.60+1.92-3.75=-0.23\). The best possible score belongs to the consensus; for CTCF it is \(26.1\) (TGGCCACCAGGGGGCGCTA). Because every position adds only a little, a window with one or two mismatches can still score high (panel b below).

docs.title: How high must a score be?
docs.text:
A window is a hit when \(S\ge t\). But how high should the cutoff \(t\) be? Strict enough that random DNA rarely passes. We say how rare with a p-value \(\pi\) (motif_pvalue, default \(10^{-5}\)): \(t\) is the smallest score for which

\[ P_0(S\ge t)\le\pi , \]

where \(P_0\) is the probability for a window of random DNA with independent, equally likely bases. In words: random DNA passes only about once in \(1/\pi\) windows. A smaller \(\pi\) means a higher \(t\) and fewer, more reliable hits.

In the toy example there are \(4^3=64\) possible windows, all equally likely at random. Only ACG scores above \(5\), so \(P_0(S\ge5)=1/64\). For CTCF there are \(4^{19}\approx 2.7\times10^{11}\) windows, far too many to list, so instead we build the distribution of the score one position at a time. Let \(f_i(s)\) be the probability that the first \(i\) positions of a random window add up to \(s\). We start with \(f_0(0)=1\) (an empty window has score \(0\)). Adding position \(i\), each of the four bases appears with probability \(1/4\) and shifts the sum by \(M_{b,i}\):

\[ f_i(s)=\frac14\sum_{b\in\{A,C,G,T\}} f_{i-1}\big(s-M_{b,i}\big). \]

In the toy example, after position 1 the possible sums are \(1.60,\,-3.75,\,-1.17,\,-1.17\), each with probability \(1/4\) (so \(-1.17\) has \(1/2\)); position 2 shifts every sum again, and so on. After the last position, the tail is added up:

\[ P_0(S\ge t)=\sum_{s\ge t}f_L(s). \]

The answer is exact (no simulation, no luck involved) and takes only \(L\) steps. To keep the number of distinct sums finite, scores are rounded to \(1/100\). For the bundled CTCF matrix this gives \(t=8.3\) for \(\pi=10^{-4}\), \(t=13.1\) for \(\pi=10^{-5}\) and \(t=17.0\) for \(\pi=10^{-6}\) (panel c below).

a The CTCF motif (JASPAR MA0139.1) as a logo: the height of a letter is how strongly that base is preferred at that position. b One window of DNA is scored by adding one number per position. c The score of a window of random DNA has a known distribution, which fixes the cutoff t.

docs.title: Two strands
docs.text:
DNA is a double helix: two strands that run in opposite directions, and a protein can sit on either of them. A site on the reverse strand reads, along the written strand, as the reverse complement of the motif: every base is swapped for its partner (\(A\leftrightarrow T\), \(C\leftrightarrow G\)) and the order is reversed. For the toy motif ACG it is CGT. Scoring the reverse-strand site therefore uses the matrix

\[ M^{-}_{b,i}=M_{\bar b,\;L+1-i}, \]

where \(\bar b\) is the partner of \(b\) and \(L+1-i\) is the mirrored position. Every window is scored twice: with \(M\) (strand \(+\), the motif as written, a forward site) and with \(M^{-}\) (strand \(-\), a reverse site). A window that contains an unknown base (N) never gives a hit.

Testing both strands doubles the number of tests, so the chance of a false hit grows. An anchor of \(n\) bp has \(2(n-L+1)\) windows, and random DNA gives at least one false hit with probability

\[ 1-(1-\pi)^{2(n-L+1)} . \]

The report compares the fraction of anchors with a hit with this number: real CTCF anchors should be much richer in motifs than random DNA.

docs.title: One probability per anchor
docs.text:
An anchor can contain several hits, on both strands, and they may disagree. What we want in the end is one number: how likely is the site to be reversed? Say the hits \(h\) have scores \(S_h\) and strands \(\sigma_h\in\{+,-\}\). Since \(2^{S_h}\) is a likelihood ratio, it measures how strong the evidence is that hit \(h\) is the true site. We define

\[ P(\mathrm{rev})=\frac{\sum_{h:\,\sigma_h=-}2^{S_h}}{\sum_{h}2^{S_h}}, \]

the share of the evidence that sits on reverse hits. It is \(0\) when all the evidence is forward and \(1\) when all of it is reverse, and a hit that is 3 points stronger simply counts \(2^3=8\) times more. In the code the weights are written \(2^{S_h-S_{\max}}\), which gives the same ratio (the common factor \(2^{-S_{\max}}\) cancels) but avoids huge numbers. An anchor without any hit gets \(P(\mathrm{rev})=-1\), meaning unknown.

For example, a \(+\) hit with \(S=17.4\) and a \(-\) hit with \(S=14.4\) have weights \(1\) and \(2^{-3}=0.125\), so \(P(\mathrm{rev})=0.125/1.125=0.11\): the site is most probably forward.

docs.title: From orientation to \(L\) and \(R\)
docs.text:
The model describes each CTCF site by two profiles along the chromosome: \(L_k\) says how strongly bead \(k\) stops legs that move left (forward sites) and \(R_k\) how strongly it stops legs that move right (reverse sites). Each loop carries a weight \(w\) (its PET count, i.e. the number of read pairs supporting it, or 1 when the file has none). Its two anchors are placed on beads, and the weight of the anchor on bead \(k\) is shared between the profiles according to its probability \(P_k\),

\[ L_k \mathrel{+}= w\,(1-P_k),\qquad R_k \mathrel{+}= w\,P_k . \]

A sure forward site (\(P_k=0\)) feeds only \(L\), a sure reverse site only \(R\), and an anchor with unknown orientation gives \(w/2\) to each. A loop whose left anchor is forward and whose right anchor is reverse is convergent, and its two legs can both stop there.

a Each window of an anchor is scored on both strands. b The hits of an anchor are combined into one probability of being reversed. c This probability divides the weight of the loop between L (red) and R (blue).

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
For every loop file the finder does the following steps, in this order.

  1. Read and filter. The BEDPE is read (at least six columns; the seventh is the PET count or score). Loops with both anchors inside the modelled region and with at least min_pet counts are kept, and identical loops are counted once.
  2. Collect anchors. The distinct anchors \((\text{chrom},\text{start},\text{end})\) of the kept loops are listed, so an anchor shared by many loops is scanned only once.
  3. Read the sequence. Each anchor, extended by motif_pad bp on both sides, is read from the reference genome. The FASTA file is indexed (a .fai file is created next to it and reused), so only the requested piece is read, never the whole genome.
  4. Scan. The windows of the anchor are scored on both strands, and every window with \(S\ge t\) is a hit. The scan adds the \(L\) shifted columns of the matrix, so it needs about \(L\) operations per base.
  5. Call. The number of hits, the best score, its strand and position and \(P(\mathrm{rev})\) are computed for the anchor.
  6. Write. The probabilities of the two anchors are written as columns 8 and 9 of an annotated BEDPE, and the model reads them as its \(L\) and \(R\) profiles.

docs.title: Using the motif finder
docs.text:
In LoopSage

The search runs in the preparation stage when a genome is given. Example: examples/02_chiapet_motif_orientation.ini.

loopsage -c config.ini --motif-genome hg38.fa
loopsage -c config.ini --motif-genome hg38.fa --motif-pvalue 1e-4 --min-pet 3
Key (option) Default Meaning motif_genome (--motif-genome) none reference genome FASTA (not compressed); turns the motif search on motif_pfm (--motif-pfm) bundled CTCF MA0139.1 motif counts, four rows A, C, G, T of equal length, or a JASPAR file motif_pvalue (--motif-pvalue) \(10^{-5}\) chance of a hit in random DNA: smaller is stricter motif_pseudocount 0.8 pseudocount \(\alpha\) added to the counts motif_pad 0 bp added on both sides of every anchor before the search min_pet (--min-pet) 0 keep only loops with at least this many PET counts or this score

Chromosome names are matched flexibly (1 and chr1 are the same). A BEDPE that already has orientation probabilities in columns 8 and 9 keeps them when no genome is given, and they are replaced when it is.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
The data folder gets the annotated loop file loops_annotated.bedpe (the six BEDPE columns, the PET count and the two probabilities, with \(-1\) for unknown), and the tables motif_loops.tsv (one row per loop) and motif_anchors.tsv (one row per anchor: number of hits, best score, strand, position and \(P(\mathrm{rev})\)), and motif_stats.json with the counts of every step. The report shows the motif, its cutoff, the fraction of anchors with a motif next to what random DNA would give, and how many loops have both, one or no oriented anchor, plus a figure with the number of loops after each step, the best score of every anchor against the cutoff, and the orientation of the left against the right anchor (convergent loops lie in one corner).

Reading the result

Most loops from CTCF experiments should have convergent anchors. If the share of anchors with a motif is close to the random value, the cutoff is probably too loose, or the anchors are not CTCF-driven, and the orientations are then not informative.

docs.title: The Optimizer
docs.text:
LoopSage has a few numbers that nobody can measure directly: how many extruders \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) are on the region, how strong the folding and the binding terms are, and how noisy the simulation is (its temperature). The optimizer is an optional stage (--optimize) that finds good values of these numbers automatically. It tries many short simulations and keeps the parameters whose simulated contact map looks most like a target map, which is either a Hi-C map or the map drawn from the input loops.

The optimizer. A short Monte Carlo run turns a parameter set θ into a loop map, the loss compares it with the target, and Nelder–Mead proposes the next θ. When the search stops, the best candidates are re-scored on longer runs and the winner is used for the production run.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
1. A parameter set \(\theta=(K,f,b,T)\) is chosen.
  2. A short Monte Carlo run with \(\theta\) produces loops, which are drawn as a contact map.
  3. The loss compares this map with the target map (compartments, decay, domains, loop size).
  4. Nelder–Mead proposes a better \(\theta\), and steps 2 to 4 repeat until the search stops.
  5. The best few candidates are re-scored on longer runs, and the winner is used for the production run.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
In LoopSage

The optimizer needs a target: a BEDPE loop file, or a Hi-C map (--hic). Run it with --optimize. The Monte Carlo stage then runs all its steps with the optimized values.

loopsage -c config.ini --optimize
loopsage -c config.ini --optimize --opt-evals 40 --opt-steps 20000 --hic sample.hic

Prefer a Hi-C target

A dense map such as Hi-C (--hic) constrains the decay, the domains and the compartments together, so the fitted values are reliable. Sparse loop data (ChIA-PET, HiChIP) hold only a few hundred dots and say little about loop length and folding; the search then tends towards small \(f\) and short loops, which is an effect of sparsity, not of the chromatin.

With loop data alone, the insulation and decay profiles are taken from the loops themselves, not from the dot map: each loop counts on all beads between its anchors (its coverage, used as the insulation profile) and at all separations up to its length (the decay), for input and simulated loops alike. The profiles are smoothed over about 100 kb, so boundaries are less sharp. Check that \(f\) and the loop sizes are plausible.

docs.title: What is fitted
docs.text:
The optimizer searches for four numbers, collected in the vector \(\theta=(K,\ f,\ b,\ T)\):

  • \(K\): the number of extruders \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) of the first family,
  • \(f\): the strength of the folding term of the energy (it depends on the loop sizes),
  • \(b\): the strength of the binding term (it rewards legs that sit on CTCF sites),
  • \(T\): a temperature scale that multiplies the whole schedule (t_init and t_final), so an annealing schedule keeps its shape.

The search runs on \(x=(K,\ln f,\ln b,\ln T)\), because \(f\), \(b\) and \(T\) act multiplicatively: doubling \(f\) matters equally at \(f=0.1\) and at \(f=1\). Every parameter stays in a box: \(f\in[0.05,3]\), \(b\in[0.25,3]\), \(T\in[1,3]\), and \(K\) between about a quarter and four times its start value \(K_0\) (never above \(N_{\mathrm{beads}}/3\)). The start is \(\theta_0=(K_0,f_0,b_0,1)\), with \(f_0,b_0\) from the configuration.

docs.title: The target and the simulated map
docs.text:
Both are \(N\times N\) contact maps \(M_{ij}\) between beads. The simulated map is built from the loops \((m,n)\) of a short Monte Carlo run: each loop gives a dot at \((m,n)\), a weaker enrichment inside it, and communication between loops that share an anchor (up to 6 loops in a chain, each step weaker by 0.6). The target map is either the denoised Hi-C map (--hic) or the input loops drawn in exactly the same way and smoothed over target_smooth beads. Each map is divided by the mean of its upper triangle, so only shape matters.

Two quantities are used below. The decay \(P(s)\) is the mean of the \(s\)-th diagonal of the map, i.e. the mean contact at separation \(s\). The observed/expected map is \(\tilde M_{ij}=M_{ij}/P(|i-j|)\): the decay is divided out, so only domains and loops remain.

docs.title: The loss
docs.text:
The loss measures how far the simulated map is from the target. It is \(0\) for a perfect match and is a weighted sum of four terms,

\[ L(\theta)=w_{\mathrm{eig}}\,L_{\mathrm{eig}}+0.5\,L_{P}+w_{\mathrm{ins}}\,L_{\mathrm{ins}}+L_{\mathrm{size}} . \]

We do not correlate the two heatmaps entry by entry. Instead we compare a few numbers that summarise a map, its components: the compartment pattern, the decay with distance, the domain boundaries and the loop size. Each term is a distance between \(0\) (identical) and about \(1\) (completely different).

Term What it compares Biological meaning Weight \(L_{\mathrm{eig}}\) leading eigenvectors (PC1, ...) of the two maps A/B compartments \(w_{\mathrm{eig}}\), grows with the region \(L_{P}\) shape of the decay \(P(s)\) how contacts fall with distance, i.e. loop length and folding \(0.5\) \(L_{\mathrm{ins}}\) insulation profiles TAD boundaries \(w_{\mathrm{ins}}\), falls with the region \(L_{\mathrm{size}}\) mean loop length loops must not collapse \(1\)

docs.title: Compartments (eigenvector term)
docs.text:
Take the correlation matrix of \(\ln(\tilde M+0.2)\), where \(\tilde M\) is the observed/expected map (each diagonal divided by its mean, so the decay drops out). Its eigenvectors are the directions along which the map varies most, and the first one is the familiar PC1 that separates compartments. Let \(u^{\mathrm{sim}}_j\) and \(u^{\mathrm{tgt}}_j\) be the first \(k=3\) eigenvectors of the two maps, paired by the size of their eigenvalues. The sign of an eigenvector is arbitrary, so we take absolute values \(|u|\) (entry by entry) and set

\[ L_{\mathrm{eig}}=1-\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^{k}\frac{|u^{\mathrm{sim}}_j|\cdot|u^{\mathrm{tgt}}_j|}{\big\||u^{\mathrm{sim}}_j|\big\|\,\big\||u^{\mathrm{tgt}}_j|\big\|} . \]

The fraction is the cosine of the angle between two vectors, between \(0\) and \(1\) here because all entries are non-negative. So \(L_{\mathrm{eig}}\) is \(0\) for the same profiles along the chromosome and \(1\) for profiles with no overlap.

With the Potts model on

When epi_coeff > 0 the compartments live in the average state \(\langle s\rangle_t\) of every bead (its Potts state averaged over the production snapshots and smoothed with a sliding window along the chain), not in the eigenvectors of the simulated map. Then \(L_{\mathrm{eig}}\) compares \(\langle s\rangle_t\) with the A/B reference, which is the leading eigenvector of the Hi-C map when there is one (otherwise the compartment track), with the sign set so that B is negative:

\[ L_{\mathrm{eig}}=\frac{1-r}{2},\qquad r=\operatorname{corr}\big(\langle s\rangle_t,\ \mathrm{PC1}^{\mathrm{ref}}\big). \]

The Pearson correlation \(r\) lies in \([-1,1]\), so the term runs from \(0\) (same A/B pattern) to \(1\) (mirror image). Without a reference the eigenvector comparison above is used.

docs.title: Decay with distance
docs.text:
\[ L_P=\operatorname{Var}_s\big[\ln P^{\mathrm{sim}}(s)-\ln P^{\mathrm{tgt}}(s)\big], \]

with a small offset \(0.02\) inside the logarithms. The variance is \(0\) when the two decays differ only by a constant factor, so \(L_P\) compares the shape of the decay, not its scale.

docs.title: Domain boundaries (insulation term)
docs.text:
The insulation \(I_i\) of bead \(i\) is the mean contact in the diamond across it, with a half-width of 100 kb (at least 5 beads), so it is low at a boundary. Each profile is rescaled to \([0,1]\), \(\hat I_i=(I_i-\min I)/(\max I-\min I)\), and

\[ L_{\mathrm{ins}}=\operatorname{mean}_i\big|\hat I^{\mathrm{sim}}_i-\hat I^{\mathrm{tgt}}_i\big| , \]

a distance between \(0\) (same profile) and \(1\) (opposite). For a target made of loops (BEDPE) the insulation and the decay are not read from the drawn map but from the loops themselves; see the note on Hi-C targets.

docs.title: Loop size
docs.text:
\[ L_{\mathrm{size}}=\max\!\Big(0,\ \Big|\log_2\frac{\tilde\ell^{\mathrm{sim}}}{\tilde\ell^{\mathrm{input}}}\Big|-1\Big), \]

with \(\tilde\ell\) the median loop length. The term is zero while the simulated median is within a factor 2 of the input median, and grows by one for every further factor 2, in either direction. Sparse loop data hardly constrain the loop size, and without it the search can drift to tiny loops, or, with the folding coefficient at its upper limit and the binding weak, to loops stacked over the whole region. The median is used instead of the mean because input loop lengths have a long tail: the mean would ask for far more nesting than the extruders can supply.

docs.title: Weights follow the region size
docs.text:
The two weights \(w_{\mathrm{eig}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{ins}}\) depend on the length of the modelled region \(S\), because the two terms describe structures of different size. TADs are domains of about 0.1–1 Mb, so in a region of a few Mb the insulation is the informative term. Compartments are blocks of a few Mb: a 5 Mb region holds at most one or two of them, so PC1 says almost nothing there. It starts to carry information when the region contains 2–3 blocks (about 10 Mb) and dominates when it contains many (30 Mb up to a whole chromosome). The switch is sharp, not linear:

\[ s=\frac{1}{1+(S_0/S)^{3}},\qquad w_{\mathrm{eig}}=2s,\qquad w_{\mathrm{ins}}=\max\big(2(1-s),\,0.25\big),\qquad S_0=30\,\mathrm{Mb}. \]

Here \(s\) is a smooth switch from \(0\) (small regions) to \(1\) (large ones), and \(S_0\) is where both weights equal \(1\).

Region \(w_{\mathrm{eig}}\) \(w_{\mathrm{ins}}\) What dominates 5 Mb 0.01 2.0 TADs and loops 10 Mb 0.07 1.9 TADs and loops 17 Mb 0.3 1.7 mostly TADs and loops 30 Mb 1.0 1.0 balanced 60 Mb 1.8 0.25 compartments 100 Mb or more 2.0 0.25 compartments

The weights used are printed in the log and shown in the report.

a The weight of the PC1 (eigenvector) term and of the insulation term against the length of the modelled region. b What a region of that size contains: TADs (triangles), A (red) and B (blue) compartment blocks, and a sketch of the chain. A small region holds a few TADs and at most one A/B block, so PC1 carries almost no information; a large region holds many blocks, which segregate in space into an A and a B cloud. c With the Potts model on, the loop-extrusion parameters are fitted first and the Potts parameters second.

docs.title: The search: Nelder–Mead
docs.text:
Every evaluation of \(L\) is a Monte Carlo run. So \(L\) has no formula and no gradient, one input (\(K\)) is an integer, and the value is noisy: two seeds give slightly different losses. A method that only needs values of \(L\) fits well, and the optimizer uses the Nelder–Mead simplex method (Nelder and Mead, 1965; the SciPy implementation follows Gao and Han, 2012).

The idea. In \(n=4\) dimensions a simplex is a set of \(n+1=5\) points \(x_{(1)},\dots,x_{(5)}\), like a triangle in 2D. Imagine that the points are hikers on a foggy hill who can only measure their own height \(L\). The one who stands highest (the worst point) walks to a better place, using what the others know. Repeating this makes the group slide downhill and shrink around a minimum.

Initial simplex. It contains the start \(x_0\) and four more points, each obtained by moving one coordinate of \(x_0\): \(K\) by \(+\max(0.3K_0,2)\), \(\ln f\) by \(-1.2\), \(\ln b\) by \(-1.2\) and \(\ln T\) by \(+0.5\).

One iteration. Sort the points so that \(L(x_{(1)})\le\dots\le L(x_{(5)})\). Write \(x_w=x_{(5)}\) for the worst point and \(c=\tfrac14\sum_{i=1}^{4}x_{(i)}\) for the centre of the other four. Then:

  1. Reflect. Mirror the worst point through the centre, \(x_r=c+(c-x_w)\), and evaluate \(L(x_r)\).
  2. Expand. If \(L(x_r)<L(x_{(1)})\) (better than all points), the direction is very good, so go twice as far: \(x_e=c+2\,(x_r-c)\). Keep the better of \(x_e\) and \(x_r\) in place of \(x_w\).
  3. Accept. If \(L(x_{(1)})\le L(x_r)<L(x_{(4)})\) (neither best nor worst), keep \(x_r\) in place of \(x_w\).
  4. Contract. If \(L(x_r)\ge L(x_{(4)})\) the step was too bold, so step back towards the centre: \(x_c=c+\tfrac12(x_r-c)\) if \(L(x_r)<L(x_w)\) (outside contraction), and \(x_c=c+\tfrac12(x_w-c)\) otherwise (inside contraction). If \(L(x_c)\) is better than the point it was compared with (\(x_r\) or \(x_w\) respectively), keep \(x_c\) in place of \(x_w\).
  5. Shrink. If the contraction did not help either, the simplex is probably around a valley floor, so every point moves halfway to the best one: \(x_{(i)}\leftarrow x_{(1)}+\tfrac12\big(x_{(i)}-x_{(1)}\big)\) for \(i=2,\dots,5\).

The factors \(1\), \(2\), \(\tfrac12\) and \(\tfrac12\) are the standard choices (reflection, expansion, contraction, shrink). In LoopSage, \(K\) is rounded to an integer and every point is clipped to the box before it is evaluated.

docs.title: One evaluation
docs.text:
An evaluation is a short run of opt_steps steps (the first quarter is burn-in, one replica, 200 snapshots, so about 150 equilibrium configurations) with a new random seed, never that of the production run. One step is a sweep over all LEFs, so the cost of an evaluation grows with the number of LEFs and the loss maps with the square of the number of beads.

Large regions. For a big region(above opt_max_beads, 1500 beads by default; 20 000 or 50 000 beads are common) the optimizer therefore simulates only the window of that many beads that holds most loops, with the LEF density kept, and the fitted number of LEFs is scaled back to the whole region. The production run then uses your own n_steps and sampling frequency.

docs.title: When the search stops
docs.text:
The search stops at the first of three events:

  • Converged: the simplex is smaller than \(0.02\) in \(x\) and the losses of its points differ by less than \(0.005\).
  • Budget: opt_evals evaluations have been used.
  • Early stopping (on by default): the best loss dropped by less than opt_min_gain (0.01) over the last opt_patience (20) evaluations. Because the loss is noisy, tiny gains do not count as progress, and the search is not wasted on noise.

docs.title: The final check
docs.text: The lowest loss of a noisy search is often a lucky one (the winner's curse). So the best three distinct candidates and the starting point are re-scored with runs three times longer and new seeds, and the lowest long-run loss wins. The result is therefore never worse than the start on the long check; if the start wins, it is kept and the report says that the optimizer "gave up".

docs.title: With the Potts model: two stages
docs.text:
When the Potts model is on and there is an A/B reference, the optimizer runs two searches in a row, so that the compartments do not disturb the fit of the loops:

  1. Loop extrusion. It fits \(K\), \(f\), \(b\) and the temperature scale with the Potts model off, using only the insulation, the decay and the loop size (\(w_{\mathrm{eig}}=0\)).
  2. Potts model. It keeps those values and fits epi_coeff (searched within a factor 10 around its start) and p_epigenetic (between 0.1 and 0.9) with the full weighted loss. The field \(h\) of the Potts model already carries the A/B pattern (from the compartment track or from the Hi-C eigenvector), so the correlation with the reference is easy to reach. What the search really decides is the balance: the coupling is increased only as far as it helps the compartments and does not harm the TAD terms. Because PC1 enters with the region-size weight, it hardly matters in a small region, where the coupling is then set mainly by not damaging the insulation.

Stage 2 uses a third of the evaluations of stage 1 (at least 10). Without an A/B reference, epi_coeff is not optimized and a warning is printed.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
The stage writes the chosen values into config_resolved.ini, marked with the source optimizer, and saves optimized_parameters.json (start and best parameters, loss terms, number of evaluations, whether the search converged). The report contains the table of the parameters before and after, the four loss terms, the best evaluations, and three figures: the convergence of the loss, the landscape explored by the search, and the target map next to the simulated one. A one-sentence verdict says whether the search converged, stopped early or used up its budget, and warns if a parameter sits at the edge of its range, because then the optimum may lie outside.

Reading the result

A loss of 0 is a perfect match, and the loss at the start is typically between 1 and 4. If the start wins the final check, the starting parameters were already as good as the search could find. If \(K\), \(f\), \(b\) or \(T\) sits at the edge of its range, the box is probably too tight for your data.

docs.title: The Pipeline
docs.text:
LoopSage turns a list of loops into three-dimensional structures in a few steps. It first reads the data, then samples many possible sets of loops with a Monte Carlo simulation, then relaxes every set into a 3D polymer with molecular dynamics, and finally compares the result with experiments. Each of these steps is a stage. This page shows how the stages follow one another, what each of them hands to the next one, and how to run all of them or just one.

The pipeline. Solid boxes always run, dashed boxes run when a flag asks for them. Every stage that produces data saves it in the run folder, so a later run can start from it.

docs.title: The stages
docs.text:
1. Preprocessing. The stage reads the loop file (BEDPE) or the CTCF peaks (BED, narrowPeak) for the chosen region and puts everything on a grid of beads, the simulation units (a bead is a piece of chromatin of a few kb). If you asked for it, it first runs the Motif Finder to find the direction of the CTCF sites. The result is a set of arrays: the anchor profiles \(L\) and \(R\) (how strongly each bead holds a left or right leg of an extruder), the loop map, optional tracks, and an optional compartment field \(h\). If a Hi-C file is given, it is read here too. See Preprocessing.

2. Optimizer (--optimize). A few numbers of the model cannot be measured: the number of extruders, the strength of the folding and the binding, the temperature. The optimizer tries many short simulations and keeps the values whose loops look most like the target (a Hi-C map or the input loops). It passes the chosen values to the next stage. See The Optimizer.

3. Monte Carlo. The core of the model. A set of \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) extruders, each one a loop between two beads, is moved at random and the moves are accepted or rejected with an energy rule. The stage saves a snapshot of all loops every few steps. See Monte Carlo.

4. Molecular dynamics (--run-MD). Every Monte Carlo snapshot is turned into a 3D structure: the loops become springs in a bead-spring polymer, which is relaxed with a Langevin simulation in OpenMM. See Molecular Dynamics.

5. 3D structure. It works on the MD frames: interactive viewer, videos, and the ensemble of structures as .cif files. It only runs together with the MD.

6. Analysis. Contact maps are built from the Monte Carlo loops and from the 3D frames, and compared with the input loops and with Hi-C when it is given (correlations, insulation, decay with distance). It also extracts map features such as TAD boundaries.

7. Links (--knots, or a topoisomerase mode). An optional topological analysis of the 3D loops (linking numbers), described in Topology.

8. Report. Everything above is collected in one report.html with the figures, tables and short explanations.

docs.title: What is passed from stage to stage
docs.text:
The stages do not talk to each other directly. They share one run context that holds the results computed so far, and each stage reads what it needs from it:

Stage Reads Produces Preprocessing the input files \(L\), \(R\), loop map, tracks, field \(h\), the Hi-C map Optimizer the inputs and the target the best \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\), \(f\), \(b\) and temperature (written into the configuration) Monte Carlo the inputs and the configuration for every snapshot: the loop positions \((m_i,n_i)\), the epigenetic states, the energy terms Molecular dynamics the snapshots for every snapshot: the 3D coordinates of all beads Analysis all of the above maps, scores, validation figures

The Monte Carlo snapshots are the bridge between the model and the 3D structure: the molecular dynamics never sees the energy of the Monte Carlo, only the final loops and states.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
A run is described by a configuration file, by command-line options, or by both (an option overrides the file). Every option has a configuration key, see the Reference.

# everything, from a config file
loopsage -c config.ini

# the same with options only
loopsage -f loops.bedpe -r chr1:78000000-92000000 -n 1000 -t 4 --run-MD -o results

# add the optimizer and a Hi-C file
loopsage -f loops.bedpe -r chr1:78000000-92000000 -n 1000 --run-MD --optimize --hic sample.hic

You can also run one stage on its own. The earlier stages are then not recomputed: their saved results are loaded from the latest run folder.

python -m loopsage.pipeline.stage_mc -c config.ini      # only the Monte Carlo, inputs are reused
python -m loopsage.pipeline.stage_md -c config.ini      # only the MD, the Monte Carlo is reused

Because the Monte Carlo result is saved, you can change only MD options (time step, forces, number of steps per frame) and repeat the MD without sampling the loops again.

docs.title: The run folder
docs.text:
Every run writes its files into its own folder, named after the region and a run number:

results/chr1_78000000_92000000_1/
  config_resolved.ini     every option used, and where its value came from
  data/                   saved stage results (inputs.npz, mc.npz, md.npz, ...)
    metadata/             maps and matrices as .npy
  structures/             init_structure.cif, trajectory.dcd, ensemble/ (one .cif per frame)
  visualizations/         all figures (png and svg), the 3D viewer, videos
  report/report.html      the report
  logs/loopsage.log       the full log

The file config_resolved.ini is the best record of a run: it contains every option, and for each one whether it was a default, came from the file, from the command line, or was set by the optimizer. With the same file and the same --seed (and --threads 1 for the MD) a run can be repeated exactly.

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text: The simulation does not work with genomic coordinates, files and read counts. It works with beads and with a few arrays of numbers per bead. The preprocessing stage is the translation: it reads the experimental files for your region and turns them into the arrays that the Monte Carlo needs. This page explains what is read, how every file type is modelled, and the two ways to turn anchor signal into an energy landscape (preferential and contrastive binding).

docs.title: What comes out
docs.text: Array Meaning Used by \(L_k\), \(R_k\) how strongly bead \(k\) holds the left leg and the right leg of an extruder (anchor profiles) binding energy \(J_{ij}\) which bead pairs are connected: the chain backbone and the input loops epigenetic coupling (static mode) \(J^{\mathrm{loss}}_{ij}\) weighted map of the input loops binding energy in the 2D mode \(h_k\) compartment field, \(+1\) for A and \(-1\) for B epigenetic energy, compartment force extra tracks BigWig signals, a loading preference for extruders extra binding energy, loading Hi-C map contact map on the bead grid validation, target of the optimizer, field \(h\)

docs.title: Region and beads
docs.text:
You choose a chromosome region and the number of beads \(N\). The region is cut into \(N\) equal pieces, and bead \(k\) stands for the \(k\)-th piece. The bead size is the region length divided by \(N\) (for 14 Mb and 1000 beads: 14 kb). If you give no number of beads, LoopSage uses one bead per 2 kb.

[input]
chrom        = chr1
region_start = 78000000
region_end   = 92000000
n_beads      = 1000          # empty: region length / 2 kb
genome       = hg38          # or hg19: only used for chromosome sizes

On the command line the region is -r chr1:78000000-92000000 and the beads -n 1000. A loop anchor is placed on the bead that contains the middle of the anchor interval; two anchors that fall on the same bead make a loop of length zero, so they are dropped.

docs.title: Loop files (BEDPE)
docs.text:
A BEDPE file has one line per loop, with the two anchors as genomic intervals:

chr1  78450000  78460000  chr1  78790000  78800000  14
#     start1    end1      #     start2    end2      score (weight)

The first six columns are the two anchors, the seventh (optional) is the weight of the loop, normally the number of read pairs (PET count) that support it. A loop with weight 14 pulls the model's attention more than a loop with weight 2. Two more optional columns (the eighth and ninth) hold the probability that each anchor's CTCF site is reversed; they are written by the Motif Finder and are the only place where the direction of the CTCF sites enters.

docs.title: From loops to \(L\) and \(R\)
docs.text:
Every loop adds its weight to the two beads of its anchors. If the directions of the CTCF sites are known, the weight of an anchor is divided between \(L\) (forward site) and \(R\) (reverse site), exactly as described in From orientation to \(L\) and \(R\). Without directions, each anchor feeds both profiles and the model decides the orientation on its own. At the end of this step \(L_k\) and \(R_k\) are large on beads where many loops start (or end) and zero elsewhere.

Three further steps make the profiles easy to use:

  1. Smoothing. A ChIA-PET anchor is a window of a few kb, but the simulation can place a leg only on a bead; a very sharp spike would either be hit exactly or missed. A Gaussian filter spreads each spike over a few neighbouring beads, with width \(\sigma=\max(1.5,\,N/300)\) beads (about 40 kb for 1000 beads over 14 Mb). It is on by default (smoothing_input = True).
  2. Mean scaling. Each profile is divided by its mean over the beads, so the average bead has value 1. After this, the numbers do not depend on how many loops the file has or on the bead size.
  3. Binding mode (next section): optionally add the coverage of the input loops, so that loop-free beads are penalised.

docs.title: The loop maps
docs.text: Besides \(L\) and \(R\) the stage keeps two \(N\times N\) matrices. \(J\) is binary: 1 on the chain backbone (neighbouring beads) and on every input loop. \(J^{\mathrm{loss}}\) keeps the weights of the loops. By default the energy uses only \(L\) and \(R\) (data_loss_mode = 0); with data_loss_mode = 1 it uses \(J^{\mathrm{loss}}\) instead, which scores a pair of legs and not each leg alone. In that mode \(J^{\mathrm{loss}}\) is smoothed with a Gaussian of width loss_sigma beads, so that the extruder legs see a continuous landscape and not isolated dots.

docs.title: Peak files (BED, narrowPeak)
docs.text: If you have only CTCF ChIP-seq peaks and no loops, give a .bed or .narrowPeak file. Each peak is a binding site with a weight (the score column); a peak spanning several beads spreads its weight over them. There are no loop pairs in such a file, so only \(L\) and \(R\) are built (the 2D mode and the loop-based optimizer target are not available). An optional probability column gives the direction of each site in the same way as for BEDPE.

docs.title: Preferential and contrastive binding
docs.text:
The profiles \(L\) and \(R\) enter the energy through the binding energy: a leg placed on a bead with a large value lowers the energy, so it is more probable (the Monte Carlo page gives the formula). What the energy should say about beads without any anchor is a modelling choice, and LoopSage offers two:

[energy]
binding_mode = preferential      # or: contrastive          (CLI: --binding-mode)

a Every loop adds its weight to the bead of its left anchor (\(L\)) and of its right anchor (\(R\)); this is the same in both modes. b Contrastive mode also measures how much the input loops cover each bead. c What a simulated loop feels at three places. Numbers are from this toy example.

Preferential binding (default). Only the anchors count: a leg is attracted to the anchors and feels nothing special elsewhere, so a loop-free region costs nothing. Its weakness is that, with few and strong anchors, the extruders can form loops over regions where the input has none.

Contrastive binding. The anchor terms are the same, and a second term is added that looks at the inside of a loop. For every bead we count how many input loops span it (its coverage) and rescale it,

\[ \hat c_k=\begin{cases}-1 & c_k<0.05\,\bar c\quad\text{(loop free)},\\[2pt] \mathrm{clip}\!\left(\dfrac{c_k}{\bar c}-1,\,0,\,1\right) & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases} \]

where \(c_k\) is the coverage of bead \(k\) and \(\bar c\) its mean. So \(\hat c_k=-1\) only on a bead that (practically) no input loop spans, \(0\) on every covered bead up to the average coverage, and up to \(+1\) at twice the average or more. A simulated loop is penalised only for beads inside it that are really loop free, and rewarded for beads that are covered more than average: beads with few but some loops cost nothing. It enters the binding energy, see Monte Carlo.

What the coverage term adds

Every extruder has one left and one right leg, so the anchor terms depend only on the shape of \(L\) and \(R\) (a constant shift would change every state equally and cancel in the Metropolis rule). The coverage term looks at the beads between the two legs, and that number differs from one loop to another, so it changes the preferred loops. It needs loops (a BEDPE file); with peaks only it has no effect, and LoopSage warns about it.

Which one to use

Start with preferential binding. If the simulated loops cover regions where the input has no loops, try contrastive. If the simulation instead collapses onto a few strong anchors and leaves most of the region empty, go back to preferential, or lower the binding coefficient \(b\).

docs.title: Extra tracks
docs.text:
Any BigWig signal (for example RNA polymerase II, H3K27ac or another cohesin ChIP) can add a binding term. Each track is averaged over the beads and smoothed with the same Gaussian as the anchor profiles \(L\) and \(R\) (width \(\sigma=\max(1.5,\,N/300)\) beads, switched by smoothing_input). Negative values are set to 0, because the energy rewards the share of the track's total signal under the legs, and a track without any signal is an error. A leg placed on a bead with a high signal is rewarded or penalised according to the strength you give the track (a negative strength rewards; the default is \(-N/10\) per track, a gentle pull next to the loops, and a larger magnitude such as \(-300\) pulls the legs clearly onto the signal). A separate BigWig can describe where extruders load on the chromatin (for example NIPBL or cohesin ChIP): the rebinding move then picks the new loop position in proportion to this track instead of uniformly.

[input]
bw_files       = rnapii.bw,h3k27ac.bw        # extra binding tracks
bw_strengths   = -100,-100                   # one per track (empty = -N_beads/10)
lef_track_file = nipbl.bw                    # loading preference of the extruders   (CLI: --lef-track)

docs.title: Hi-C
docs.text:
A Hi-C file (.hic) is not needed to run the model, but it adds three things: a reference for the validation, a target for the optimizer, and, when the epigenetic model is on, the compartments.

loopsage -f loops.bedpe -r chr1:78000000-92000000 -n 1000 \
         --hic sample.hic --hic-norm KR --hic-resolution 10000

docs.title: Reading the map
docs.text:
The file is read with hic-straw, in a separate process (the library can crash the interpreter when a resolution or a normalisation is missing, and a crash must only fail one attempt). The stage tries the resolutions closest to the bead size first (an equal or finer one is preferred, because it can be summed into beads), and the normalisations in the order KR, SCALE, VC_SQRT, VC, NONE, starting with the one you asked for. Whatever it finally used is written to the report. The matrix is then put on the bead grid: finer bins are summed into beads, coarser bins are spread over the beads they cover (with a correction, so the total contact count is kept). Beads for which less than half of the Hi-C rows have data are masked (set to missing), so they do not distort the comparison.

[input]
hic_file       = sample.hic
hic_norm       = KR          # falls back to SCALE, VC_SQRT, VC, NONE
hic_resolution = 0           # bp; 0 = automatic, closest to the bead size

docs.title: Compartments from Hi-C
docs.text:
The Potts field \(h_k\) tells the epigenetic model which beads are A (positive) and which are B (negative). It comes from the first source that is available:

  1. a BigWig of the A/B signal (comp_bw_file), smoothed with track_smooth beads like the Hi-C eigenvector and rescaled to \([-1,1]\);
  2. a BED of compartments or sub-compartments (comp_bed_file): A labels count positive and B negative, deeper sub-compartments (A.2 against A.1) count a bit more, and a score column, if present, is used as \(2s-1\);
  3. the Hi-C map itself, when the epigenetic model is on (epi_coeff greater than 0) and no track is given.

In the Hi-C case the compartments are the usual PC1. From the map we divide out the decay with distance, which gives the observed/expected map. The correlation matrix of its rows says which beads contact the same partners, and its leading eigenvector (PC1) splits the beads into two groups. The sign is chosen so that the group with denser short-range contacts is B (negative), the usual convention. The values are clipped to a robust range and scaled to \([-1,1]\).

[input]
comp_bw_file  = compartments.bw      # A/B signal
comp_bed_file = subcompartments.bed  # or a BED of (sub)compartments

docs.title: Everything in one place
docs.text:
[input]
interaction_file = loops.bedpe        # .bedpe, .bed or .narrowPeak       (CLI: -f)
chrom = chr1;  region_start = 78000000;  region_end = 92000000;  n_beads = 1000
min_pet          = 0                  # BEDPE: drop loops with fewer PET counts
smoothing_input  = True               # Gaussian smoothing of L and R
hic_file         = sample.hic         # optional
motif_genome     = hg38.fa            # optional: CTCF directions (see Motif Finder)

[energy]
binding_mode     = preferential       # or contrastive
data_loss_mode   = 0                  # 0 = profiles L and R, 1 = 2D loop map
loss_sigma       = 2.0                # smoothing of the 2D map, in beads

docs.title: What is LoopSage?
docs.text: LoopSage is a program that turns a list of chromatin loops into an ensemble of 3D genome structures. It models how the protein complex cohesin pushes DNA through itself and builds loops, and it checks the result against your data.

docs.title: The idea in one minute
docs.text:
Inside the cell nucleus, DNA is folded. A key part of the folding is loop extrusion: a ring-shaped protein complex (cohesin) lands on the chromatin fibre and slides along it, pulling in DNA and growing a loop. It stops at roadblocks, mainly CTCF proteins bound to specific DNA sites, which are called anchors of the loop.

LoopSage reproduces this process in a computer:

  1. Input. You give the loops measured in an experiment (for example ChIA-PET, HiChIP or Hi-C loops) and a genomic region.
  2. Loop extrusion model. Each cohesin is a loop-extruding factor (LEF), a pair of legs on the chromatin fibre. A Monte Carlo algorithm moves the legs at random and keeps moves that make the loops agree better with your data. After many steps it has produced many plausible loop configurations, an ensemble.
  3. 3D structures. A short molecular dynamics simulation turns every loop configuration into a 3D polymer structure.
  4. Checks. The simulated contacts are compared with the experiment (loop strength, contact decay with distance, insulation score, compartments).
  5. Report. Everything is collected in one HTML report with figures, tables and plain-language explanations.

docs.title: Words used in these notes
docs.text: Term Meaning Bead One piece of the chromatin fibre in the model, covering a fixed stretch of DNA (for example 2 kb). The region is a chain of beads. Loop A pair of beads (left leg, right leg) held together by a LEF. Anchor A bead where loops tend to start or stop, typically a CTCF site. LEF Loop-extruding factor, the model of one cohesin complex. Monte Carlo (MC) A method that explores many configurations by random moves, accepting or rejecting each move with a probability set by an energy. Energy A number that is low when the loops agree with the data and with the physics of the model. Low-energy configurations are more likely. MD Molecular dynamics, a physical simulation of the 3D polymer. PET Paired-end tag, one sequencing read pair that supports a loop. More PET counts means a more reliable loop. BEDPE A text file format with one loop per line: two genomic intervals (the two anchors) plus a score.

docs.title: What you give and what you get
docs.text:
Input

  • A loop file: .bedpe (loops), or .bed / .narrowPeak (CTCF sites).
  • A region, for example chr1:77000000-95000000.
  • Optional: CTCF orientation (inside the BEDPE file, or read from a reference genome by LoopSage), BigWig tracks, a compartment track.

Output (in one folder per run)

  • report/report.html, the full report with figures and explanations.
  • visualizations/, every figure as PNG and SVG.
  • structures/, 3D structures (.cif), an interactive 3D viewer and videos.
  • data/, the numerical results; maps are saved as .npy files in data/metadata/.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
loopsage -f loops.bedpe -r chr1:77000000-95000000

Then open results/chr1_77000000_95000000_1/report/report.html in a browser. Install the program first: see Installation. To learn why LoopSage is built the way it is, read the Inspiration. All options are listed in the Reference.
