docs.title: Inspiration
docs.text: LoopSage is the first model I built and published on my own, as a first-year PhD student. I wanted chromatin modelling to be easier and friendlier to use, and I hoped to understand it from the first principles of biology.

docs.title: First principles
docs.text:
A first principle is a basic law that holds everywhere and needs no data from the system you study. In physics, a few such laws are enough to predict a lot. Take an ideal gas in a box: knowing only its temperature, volume and number of particles, the laws of physics give its pressure. It does not matter where the box is or what happened to the gas before.

When I started, I hoped chromatin could be treated in the same way: write down the basic rules of how cohesin and CTCF behave, and let the 3D genome follow from them.

docs.title: Why biology does not work like this
docs.text:
In a cell, the basic rules are not enough. Consider two cells of the same person, a liver cell and a neuron. Both contain the same DNA, and both obey the same laws of physics. Yet their genomes fold differently, because they differ in the information they carry: which genes are active, which proteins are bound to the DNA, and where CTCF sits and in which direction it points.

This information is not given by any law. It is the result of a long history of evolution and development, and the only way to know it is to measure it. In this sense a biological system is information plus physics.

What it gives Where it comes from Physics how a polymer moves, how cohesin extrudes a loop, how CTCF blocks it equations; the same in every cell Information which loops and anchors exist, which regions are active or inactive measurements such as Hi-C, ChIA-PET and ChIP-seq; different in every cell type

docs.title: What follows for modelling
docs.text:
Since the information cannot be derived, a chromatin model cannot be purely first-principles. It has to be driven by data, and it describes one biological case at a time: a given region, in a given cell type, under given conditions. The physics tells the model how the system can move, and the data tell it what the system is.

LoopSage follows this view. Loop extrusion and polymer mechanics are its engine, and the information is its input: the loops, the CTCF orientations, the compartments and the tracks that you provide. LoopSage does not explain why a loop exists. It asks which 3D structures are consistent with the loops seen in the data, and how well the result agrees with experiment.

docs.title: The gaps LoopSage tries to fill
docs.text:
Working with loop extrusion models, and talking with other researchers who build and use them, I noticed two gaps in the field. LoopSage is a modest attempt to narrow them, not a complete solution.

The first gap is validation. Chromatin models are rarely tested against experiment in a common, transparent way. A model usually reproduces the data it was tuned on, and it is seldom clear where it fails. Every model is perfectly imperfect, but without validation it is hard to say how.

The second gap is documentation and benchmarking. At the first international 4D Nucleome Hackathon in Seattle, our team compared several chromatin models on the same genomic region. We found that many of them are thinly documented, and that technical limits (different inputs, formats and assumptions) make a fair comparison difficult (Kubica et al., PLOS Computational Biology, 2025).

docs.title: How LoopSage answers
docs.text:
LoopSage tries to address both openly. Its validation is transparent: every figure states how the simulation compares with the experiment. A clean optimizer fits the parameters to your data, and the report lets a reader check the strengths and weaknesses of the model.

Running many settings is meant to be easy, so that models can be benchmarked and their parameters optimized to give better results. Much remains to be improved, and this is the direction I hope LoopSage keeps following.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer.
  • A Linux, macOS or Windows (WSL) computer. A GPU is optional: it only speeds up the 3D molecular dynamics stage.
  • About 2 GB of free disk space for the packages.

docs.title: Step by step (recommended: conda)
docs.text:
openmm (the molecular dynamics engine) and pyBigWig install most reliably from conda, so the packages are installed in two parts. hic-straw, which reads .hic files for the optional --hic reference, is installed with the package; it builds from source when no wheel exists for your system and then needs a C++ compiler and libcurl.

# 1. get the code
git clone https://github.com/SFGLab/pyLoopSage.git
cd pyLoopSage

# 2. create an isolated environment
conda create -n loopsage python=3.11 -y
conda activate loopsage

# 3. packages that are best installed from conda
conda install -c conda-forge "openmm>=8.5.1" pybigwig -y

# 4. all other packages
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 5. install pyLoopSage itself (creates the `loopsage` command)
pip install -e .

Check the installation with loopsage -h. The same command also runs as python -m loopsage.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
Run the small demo (under a minute) and open the report it writes:

python demo/run_demo.py quick

The demo uses a small synthetic loop file shipped with the repository. It needs no downloads.

To run the automatic tests (several minutes):

python -m pytest

docs.title: Choosing the 3D computing platform
docs.text: The 3D stage runs on the fastest platform it finds, in this order: CUDA (NVIDIA GPU), OpenCL, then CPU with all cores. The chosen platform is always printed. To force one, use --platform CUDA, --platform OpenCL or --platform CPU.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
A Dockerfile with CUDA support is in the repository root:

docker build -t loopsage .
docker run --gpus all -it -v "$PWD":/app loopsage

Inside the container, run LoopSage as described above.

docs.title: Optional: CTCF motif search
docs.text: To let LoopSage read CTCF orientation from a reference genome (--motif-genome), you only need a genome FASTA file, for example hg38.fa. No extra package is needed; the motif table (JASPAR MA0139.1) is included. See the CLI reference.

docs.title: Building these notes
docs.text:
The documentation is written in Markdown in the markdown/ folder and built with MkDocs:

pip install mkdocs-material
mkdocs serve          # preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build          # write the site to site/

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Complete lists of everything you can set when running LoopSage, and the three ways to run it.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: LoopSage can be used in three ways. They run the same model with the same parameters, so you can start with the one that suits you and change later.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Everything is given as options. Good for a quick run or a script.

loopsage -f loops.bedpe -r chr1:77000000-95000000 --mc-steps 20000

The results (figures, report, structures) are written to a run folder, results/chr1_77000000_95000000_1/. All options are listed on the command-line page.

docs.title: Config file
docs.text:
The settings are written in a text file, which is easy to keep, share and repeat. The command-line options still work and win over the file.

# config.ini
[input]
interaction_file = loops.bedpe
chrom = chr1
region_start = 77000000
region_end = 95000000

[monte_carlo]
n_steps = 20000

loopsage -c config.ini

The run writes the same run folder as before, including config_resolved.ini with every setting that was used. All keys are listed on the config page.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Each step is a function and the results are Python objects, so you can work in a notebook or script without writing files. Inputs are given as file paths.

import loopsage as ls

cfg = ls.config(region="chr1:77000000-95000000", n_beads=120, n_steps=20000)
geom = ls.geometry(cfg)
inputs = ls.read_inputs(cfg, geom, loops="loops.bedpe")
mc = ls.run_mc(cfg, inputs, geom)                        # Monte Carlo loop extrusion
ls.results.mean_loop_length(mc, geom)                    # a result as an array

The functions, the results and the sandbox are described on the Python page.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
Page What it covers Data input Which files LoopSage reads, how each must look (columns, examples), and which are mandatory or optional. Command-line interface The loopsage command, its general options and every option by topic, with defaults. Python interface Installing with pip and calling LoopSage from Python (import loopsage as ls): one function per step, results as arrays and figures, and a sandbox for synthetic systems. Config files How to write a .ini config file, and a table of every key (including the advanced ones that have no command-line option). Sensitivity scans The loopsage-scan command: why scanning parameters gives biophysical insight, how to write a scan file, phase transitions and bifurcations, topology, and the report.

The command-line and config pages are generated from the same parameter list in the code, so they always agree with the program.

docs.title: Command-line interface
docs.text:
LoopSage is run with one command. Every option below can also be written in a config file; the command line always wins.

loopsage [options]

Where options are read from

From weakest to strongest: built-in defaults, then the config file (-c), then command-line options, then -s KEY=VALUE. So a config file holds your usual settings and the command line changes one thing at a time.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Minimal run: a loop file and a region
loopsage -f loops.bedpe -r chr1:77000000-95000000

# Everything from a config file, but without the 3D stage and with info messages
loopsage -c config.ini --no-run-MD -vv

# Read CTCF orientation from the genome, keep loops with at least 3 PET counts, 4 threads
loopsage -f loops.bedpe -r chr1:77000000-95000000 --motif-genome hg38.fa --min-pet 3 -t 4

# Set any config key that has no option of its own
loopsage -c config.ini -s epi_coeff=0.5 -s bind_coeff=2

docs.title: General options
docs.text: Option What it does -h, --help Show the help text and exit. -c FILE, --config FILE Read settings from a sectioned .ini file (see Config files). -r CHR:START-END, --region CHR:START-END Genomic region in base pairs, for example chr1:75000000-95000000. -v, -vv, -vvv Console detail. None: main steps and progress bars. -v: plus tables. -vv: plus info messages. -vvv: plus debug. -s KEY=VALUE, --set KEY=VALUE Set any config key from the command line. Can be repeated.

docs.title: Options by topic
docs.text: Switches that are on or off come in pairs: --run-MD turns a step on and --no-run-MD turns it off. Lists in the Type column show the unit in brackets when the value has one.

docs.title: Input data and genomic region

docs.text: Option Type (unit) Default What it does --mc-steps integer (MC steps) 20000 Total Monte Carlo steps --sample-every integer (MC steps) 200 Save one snapshot every this many steps --burnin integer (MC steps) 1000 Burn-in period discarded from statistics --t-init number (a.u.) 3.0 Initial temperature --t-final number (a.u.) 1.0 Final temperature (Annealing only) --method text Annealing Sampling method --n-lef integer (LEFs) (empty) Loop extrusion factors (empty = N_anchors / 2) --lef-rw / --no-lef-rw true / false True LEF legs slide as a random walk (True) or only extrude outward (False) --lef-speed text constant Initial LEF speeds: constant (all equal), maxwell (Maxwell-Boltzmann), lognormal, or two_state (slow and fast LEFs); mean speed is always 1 --lef-speed-spread number 0.5 lognormal only: width (sigma of ln speed) --lef-fast-fraction number 0.2 two_state only: fraction of fast LEFs --lef-fast-ratio number 5.0 two_state only: speed of fast LEFs relative to slow ones

docs.text: Option Type (unit) Default What it does --run-MD / --no-run-MD true / false True Run the 3D molecular dynamics stage --platform text auto OpenMM platform: auto (try CUDA, then OpenCL, then parallel CPU), CUDA, OpenCL, CPU or Reference --init-structure text rw Initial polymer shape --step-size number (fs) 100.0 Integrator time step --md-steps integer (MD steps) 5000 MD steps per MC snapshot (per frame) --temperature number (K) 310.0 Simulation temperature

docs.text: Option Type (unit) Default What it does --render-3d / --no-render-3d true / false True Write 3d_viewer.html and videos of the 3D trajectory

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Option Type (unit) Default What it does --track-smooth number (beads) 7.0 Gaussian smoothing of the Hi-C insulation score and of the A/B track (Hi-C eigenvector or compartment BigWig) used as input and for validation (0 = off)

docs.title: Parameter optimizer
docs.text: Option Type (unit) Default What it does --optimize / --no-optimize true / false False Before the run, fit the number of LEFs, folding and binding coefficients with Nelder-Mead on short Monte Carlo runs (n_lef of the first family, f, b and the temperature schedule), then run with them --opt-evals integer (evaluations) 60 Maximum number of short Monte Carlo evaluations of the optimizer --opt-early-stop / --no-opt-early-stop true / false True Stop the optimizer early when the loss no longer improves --opt-interactive / --no-opt-interactive true / false True Pressing Enter during the optimizer shows the best parameters so far and asks whether to keep them and stop (only in a terminal) --opt-patience integer (evaluations) 20 Early stopping: evaluations without a real improvement (see opt_min_gain) before the optimizer stops --opt-steps integer (MC steps) 4000 Monte Carlo steps of one optimizer evaluation (each step is a sweep over all LEFs; the first quarter is burn-in, 200 snapshots; the final candidate check runs 3x longer) --opt-max-beads integer (beads) 1500 Largest region the optimizer simulates: bigger regions are optimized on the window of this many beads with most loops, and the number of LEFs is scaled back to the full region --target-smooth number (beads) 0.8 Smoothing of the optimizer target built from the input loops, so that the sparse loops look like a Hi-C map (0 = none) --hic-denoise number (beads) 1.0 Denoising of the Hi-C target of the optimizer, to bring out the TAD pattern (0 = none); validation always uses the raw map

docs.title: Topology
docs.text: Option Type (unit) Default What it does --knots / --no-knots true / false False Optional linking analysis of loops in 3D (slow; off by default)

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Every run gets its own folder, results/<chrom>_<start>_<end>_<run>/, with the report in report/report.html, the figures in visualizations/, the 3D structures in structures/, and the numerical results in data/ (matrices in data/metadata/ as .npy files). Use -o to choose another results folder and --run N to fix the run number.

Everything is saved by default, from the command line and from a config file. Each kind of output has its own switch to turn it off (--no-..., or ... = False in the config file):

Output Where Switch to turn it off HTML report report/report.html --no-report Figures (PNG and SVG) visualizations/ --no-figures Matrices as .npy (contact maps, distances, strengths) data/metadata/ --no-metadata 3D structures: every MD frame as .cif, start structure, topology, trajectory structures/ --no-save-ensemble 3D viewer and videos visualizations/3d/ --no-render-3d

The results of the stages (data/*.npz), the log and config_resolved.ini are always written, because the stages and the repeatability of a run depend on them. From Python, the step functions (ls.run_mc, ls.run_md, ...) write nothing; ls.run writes the same run folder as the command.

docs.title: Run only some stages
docs.text:
The pipeline has seven stages: reading the input, Monte Carlo, molecular dynamics, 3D structure analysis, validation, linking analysis and the report. Each stage can also be started alone with the same options; it re-uses the saved result of the earlier stages from the latest run.

python -m loopsage.pipeline.stage_mc -c config.ini      # Monte Carlo (and the input before it)
python -m loopsage.pipeline.stage_md -c config.ini      # up to the 3D molecular dynamics

docs.title: Config files
docs.text:
A config file keeps all the settings of a run in one place, so a run can be repeated exactly. Pass it with -c:

loopsage -c config.ini

config_example.ini in the repository root lists every key with its default and a one-line description. Copy it and change what you need.

docs.title: How to write one
docs.text:
A config file is a plain text file in the INI format: sections in square brackets, and one key = value per line.

[input]
interaction_file = /data/loops.bedpe   ; the loops to model
chrom = chr1
region_start = 77000000                ; in base pairs
region_end = 95000000

[monte_carlo]
n_steps = 20000
method = Annealing

[molecular_dynamics]
run_md = True

Rules:

  • Sections group the keys by topic (tables below). A key must be written in its own section.
  • Comments are whole lines starting with # or ;. A comment may also follow a value on the same line, after ;.
  • Empty values (seed =) mean "not set": LoopSage then picks a sensible automatic value.
  • Booleans are written True / False (also yes / no, 1 / 0).
  • Lists are comma-separated: bw_files = a.bw, b.bw.
  • Units may follow a number (step_size = 100 fs); the unit of each key is given in the tables.
  • Only the keys you change are needed. Anything missing takes its default.
  • Every command-line option is also a config key, but not the other way round: the config file has more (advanced) keys, marked ini only below.

Check what was used

Each run saves the full list of settings it used in config_resolved.ini inside the run folder, so any run can be reproduced from its own folder.

docs.title: Using the settings from Python
docs.text:
The same keys work in Python, written by name (n_steps, not the option --mc-steps):

import loopsage as ls

cfg = ls.config("config.ini", n_steps=5000, run_md=False)    # a validated Config; keyword arguments win over the file
geom = ls.geometry(cfg)
inputs = ls.read_inputs(cfg, geom, loops="loops.bedpe")      # inputs as file paths
mc = ls.run_mc(cfg, inputs, geom)                            # one function per step, results as Python objects

Values are converted exactly as in a config file, a wrong key or value raises ValueError, and cfg.as_dict() lists every setting. The full description (inputs, optimizer, Monte Carlo, molecular dynamics, results, figures, the sandbox) is on the page Python interface.

docs.text:
Section [optimizer] of the config file.

Key / CLI option Type (unit) Default What it does optimize--optimize true / false False Before the run, fit the number of LEFs, folding and binding coefficients with Nelder-Mead on short Monte Carlo runs (n_lef of the first family, f, b and the temperature schedule), then run with them opt_evals--opt-evals integer (evaluations) 60 Maximum number of short Monte Carlo evaluations of the optimizer opt_early_stop--opt-early-stop true / false True Stop the optimizer early when the loss no longer improves opt_interactive--opt-interactive true / false True Pressing Enter during the optimizer shows the best parameters so far and asks whether to keep them and stop (only in a terminal) opt_patience--opt-patience integer (evaluations) 20 Early stopping: evaluations without a real improvement (see opt_min_gain) before the optimizer stops opt_min_gainini only number 0.01 Early stopping: smallest drop of the best loss that counts as an improvement (the loss is about 1-4 at the start) opt_steps--opt-steps integer (MC steps) 4000 Monte Carlo steps of one optimizer evaluation (each step is a sweep over all LEFs; the first quarter is burn-in, 200 snapshots; the final candidate check runs 3x longer) opt_max_beads--opt-max-beads integer (beads) 1500 Largest region the optimizer simulates: bigger regions are optimized on the window of this many beads with most loops, and the number of LEFs is scaled back to the full region target_smooth--target-smooth number (beads) 0.8 Smoothing of the optimizer target built from the input loops, so that the sparse loops look like a Hi-C map (0 = none) hic_denoise--hic-denoise number (beads) 1.0 Denoising of the Hi-C target of the optimizer, to bring out the TAD pattern (0 = none); validation always uses the raw map

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
Section [topology] of the config file.

Key / CLI option Type (unit) Default What it does detect_knots--knots true / false False Optional linking analysis of loops in 3D (slow; off by default) knots_strideini only integer (frames) 10 Use every n-th MD frame for linking numbers ev_pini only number 0.0 Topoisomerase ('random' mode): probability/fraction of beads with excluded volume off during a frame continuous_topini only true / false False Topoisomerase ('random' mode) acts on one continuous stretch topo_modeini only text random Topoisomerase model: 'random' (beads with EV off for a whole frame, set by ev_p) or 'local' (short strand-passage events at close contacts) topo_rateini only number (events) 5.0 'local' mode: strand-passage attempts per MD frame per 1000 beads topo_radiusini only number (bond lengths) 2.0 'local' mode: strands closer than this can pass through each other topo_widthini only integer (beads) 3 'local' mode: beads of the passing strand that lose their excluded volume topo_windowini only number (fraction) 0.05 'local' mode: share of the frame's MD steps with excluded volume off, per attempt topo_keepini only number 1.0 'local' mode: probability to keep a passage that creates a new link between loops (1 = no bias; below 1 the topoisomerase simplifies the topology) track_crossingsini only true / false False Count chain crossings during the MD (checks whether the excluded volume leaks); also on with --knots track_everyini only integer (MD steps) 100 MD steps between crossing checks ev_barrier_targetini only number (kT) 10.0 Strand-crossing barrier used for the suggested ev_ff_strength in the topology report

docs.title: Data input
docs.text:
This page lists the files LoopSage reads, what each one must look like, and which ones you need. In short: one file with loops or peaks, and a region, are enough. Everything else is optional and each optional file adds a feature.

All text files are plain tab-separated (spaces also work for BEDPE) with no header line. Lines starting with # are ignored. Coordinates are 0-based, half-open (the BED convention), in base pairs. Chromosome names chr1 and 1 are treated as the same.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Input Required? Format Config key / CLI flag What it gives Loops or peaks Mandatory .bedpe, .bed or .narrowPeak interaction_file / -f Anchor sites and loop weights: the main input of the model Region Mandatory chr:start-end chrom, region_start, region_end / -r The stretch of genome to simulate. Only chrom is strictly needed: without start and end the whole chromosome is used (with a warning) Genome assembly Optional hg38 or hg19 genome Chromosome lengths. Default hg38 Hi-C map Optional .hic hic_file / --hic Reference for validation, and the target of the optimizer BigWig binding tracks Optional .bw bw_files, bw_strengths Extra binding energy from other factors Loading track Optional .bw lef_track_file / --lef-track Where extruders prefer to load Compartments Optional .bw or .bed comp_bw_file or comp_bed_file A/B attraction in the 3D stage Reference genome Optional FASTA (.fa, not compressed) motif_genome / --motif-genome CTCF motif search to set anchor orientations (BEDPE only) Motif matrix Optional PFM text motif_pfm / --motif-pfm Replaces the bundled CTCF motif Force field Optional OpenMM XML forcefield_path Replaces the bundled force field Config file Optional .ini -c All settings in one file, see Config files

Minimal run

loopsage -f loops.bedpe -r chr1:77000000-95000000
Nothing else is needed. The number of beads defaults to the region length divided by 2 kb (at least 10).

docs.title: Which data is used for what
docs.text:
LoopSage works in two steps, and the files feed different ones. In the Monte Carlo step the model decides which sets of loops are likely. In the molecular dynamics step it folds the polymer into 3D structures. The figure shows each file on one toy region; every file is first read onto the same grid of beads.

The input files on a toy region of 40 beads. The dashed lines mark the anchors. On the right is what each file becomes in the model. Data Which part of the model In plain words Loops (BEDPE) Monte Carlo, binding energy Says where loops can end and how strongly. Extruder legs are rewarded for sitting on anchors with many supporting reads CTCF sites (BED, narrowPeak, motif search) Monte Carlo, binding energy Same idea when you have no loops, only binding sites. The orientation (forward or reverse) tells which leg of a ring may stop at the site Binding tracks (BigWig) Monte Carlo, extra binding term Other proteins that stop or anchor extruders. Each track has its own strength Loading track (BigWig) Monte Carlo, rebinding move Says where new rings are loaded. Without it, loading is uniform along the region Compartments (BigWig or BED) Monte Carlo epigenetic term and 3D attraction Marks beads as A (active) or B (inactive). Like-type beads attract in the 3D step, so compartments separate. If you give none, they can be taken from the Hi-C map when the epigenetic model is on Hi-C map (.hic) Validation and optimizer A reference, not an input of the simulation. It is compared with the predicted map, and --optimize tunes the energy coefficients to match it Reference genome and motif Preprocessing Finds CTCF motifs in the anchors, so the orientation is known without columns 8 and 9 Force field (XML) Molecular dynamics Defines the polymer (bonds, stiffness, excluded volume)

Loops versus peaks

A loop file tells the model which pairs of sites interact. A peak file only tells which sites exist, so the model predicts the loops itself. Give loops whenever you have them.

docs.title: Loops and peaks (mandatory)
docs.text: LoopSage chooses the reader from the file extension (.bedpe, .bed, .narrowPeak, case-insensitive). Any other extension is an error. Only features that lie inside the region are used.

docs.title: BEDPE: loops
docs.text:
One loop per line, with both anchors. This is the usual output of loop callers and of ChIA-PET / HiChIP pipelines.

Column Content Needed? 1-3 chromosome, start, end of the first anchor yes 4-6 chromosome, start, end of the second anchor yes 7 weight (PET count or score) optional 8 probability that the first anchor is a reverse CTCF site optional 9 the same for the second anchor optional 
chr14   23050000  23055000  chr14  23120000  23125000  18  0.08  0.92
chr14   23180000  23185000  chr14  23260000  23265000  42  0.15  0.88
  • Both anchors must lie inside the region. Loops with an anchor outside are dropped, as are identical duplicates and lines whose coordinates are not numbers.
  • Weight (column 7): stronger loops weigh more. Without it all loops count equally. min_pet / --min-pet keeps only loops with at least that weight.
  • Orientation (columns 8, 9): a value in \([0,1]\) is the probability that the anchor is a reverse site, or -1 for unknown. Without these columns, or for -1, an anchor counts as equally likely forward or reverse. You can have LoopSage fill them in from the genome sequence with motif_genome (see below).

docs.title: BED: peaks
docs.text:
One binding site per line (for example CTCF ChIP-seq peaks). Loops are not given, so the sites define where loops may end.

Column Content Needed? 1-3 chromosome, start, end yes 5 score, used as the binding weight optional 7 probability that the site is a reverse site (-1 = unknown) optional 
chr14   23051200  23052800  site_1  1842  .  0.10

docs.title: narrowPeak: ENCODE peaks
docs.text:
The standard 10-column ENCODE peak format.

Column Content Needed? 1-3 chromosome, start, end yes 5, 7 score; signalValue (column 7) is preferred as the weight optional 10 summit offset from the start; places the site on the bead of the summit optional 11 optional extra column: probability that the site is a forward site (stored as reverse = 1 − value) optional 
chr14   23051200  23052800  peak_1  1842  .  18.23  187.42  184.20  780

Which one should I use?

Use BEDPE if you have loops, because the model then also learns which anchors are paired. Use BED or narrowPeak if you only have binding sites; the model then predicts the loops that these sites can make. min_pet and motif_genome work for BEDPE only.

docs.title: Hi-C map (optional)
docs.text:
A .hic file (Juicer format), read with the hic-straw package (installed with LoopSage). It is used as a reference to compare the predicted map to, and as the target for --optimize. It is never needed to run the model.

  • LoopSage picks the file resolution closest to the bead size (hic_resolution = 0); set a bin size in bp to choose it yourself.
  • hic_norm is KR by default. If that normalisation is missing it falls back to SCALE, VC_SQRT, VC and finally NONE.
  • The map is rebinned onto the beads. Beads without data are masked, not treated as zero.
  • A file that cannot be opened, or has no usable data for the region, stops the run with a clear message.

docs.title: BigWig tracks (optional)
docs.text:
Signal files (.bw, .bigWig) read with pyBigWig. The chromosome must exist in the file. Values are averaged per bead; negative values are set to zero. With smoothing_input on (default), they are smoothed slightly.

Use Key Meaning Binding tracks bw_files, bw_strengths One or more tracks (comma-separated) that add binding energy, for example other architectural proteins. bw_strengths gives one strength per track; if omitted, each track gets a default strength. A different number of strengths and tracks is an error Loading track lef_track_file Where extruders are loaded, for example a cohesin loader ChIP-seq. Without it, loading is uniform Compartments comp_bw_file An A/B signal, scaled to \([-1,1]\) (positive = A, negative = B)

docs.title: Compartments as BED (optional)
docs.text:
An alternative to the BigWig: comp_bed_file. Give only one of comp_bw_file and comp_bed_file.

Column Content Needed? 1-3 chromosome, start, end yes 4 label starting with A or B; sub-compartments such as A.1.2 are accepted yes 5 score in \([0,1]\), mapped to \(2\cdot\text{score}-1\) optional 
chr1   77000000  77900000  A  0.70  .
chr1   77900000  79750000  B  0.08  .

If no row overlaps the region, the run stops with an error.

docs.title: Reference genome and motif (optional)
docs.text:
With motif_genome set (BEDPE input only), LoopSage scans every anchor for CTCF motifs on both strands and writes the orientation probabilities for you, instead of reading columns 8 and 9.

  • FASTA: an uncompressed reference genome (.fa, .fasta). A .fai index is built next to the file on the first use (if the folder is writable) and reused later. Compressed .gz files are not supported: decompress them first. Chromosome names are matched with or without chr. Anchors on a chromosome missing from the FASTA get no orientation.
  • PFM (motif_pfm): by default the bundled JASPAR CTCF matrix (MA0139.1) is used. To use another motif, give a text file with four rows (A, C, G, T) of equal length. Plain numbers or the JASPAR style A [ 4 19 ... ] are both accepted, and > header lines are skipped.
  • Tuning: motif_pvalue (hit cutoff, default \(10^{-5}\), smaller is stricter), motif_pseudocount (default 0.8) and motif_pad (extend each anchor by this many bp).

docs.title: Force field (optional)
docs.text: forcefield_path points to an OpenMM force-field XML. The bundled one is used by default, and you only need your own to change the polymer model itself.

docs.title: What happens when something is wrong
docs.text: Situation Result No interaction_file, or the file does not exist Error, run stops Extension is not .bedpe, .bed or .narrowPeak Error No chromosome given, or an unknown chromosome Error Region start/end missing Whole chromosome used, with a warning Both comp_bw_file and comp_bed_file Error bw_strengths count differs from bw_files count Error min_pet or motif_genome with BED / narrowPeak Error motif_genome or motif_pfm file missing Error Orientation columns that are not probabilities Warning, columns ignored min_pet set but BEDPE has no weight column Warning, filter skipped .hic cannot be read Error with the reason

docs.title: The same inputs in Python
docs.text:
In the Python interface the inputs are passed to read_inputs, either as file paths or as arrays (useful for synthetic data).

import loopsage as ls

cfg = ls.config(region="chr1:77000000-95000000", n_beads=120)
geom = ls.geometry(cfg)

# from files
inputs = ls.read_inputs(cfg, geom, loops="loops.bedpe",
                        compartments="comps.bed", tracks=["ctcf.bw"], lef_track="nipbl.bw")

# from arrays (positions in bp)
inputs = ls.read_inputs(cfg, geom, loops=(left, right, weight))
inputs = ls.read_inputs(cfg, geom, sites=dict(position=pos, weight=w, reverse=p))

Give loops or sites, not both. See the config page for every key and the Preprocessing page for how the inputs become bead profiles.

docs.title: Python interface
docs.text:
After pip install pyLoopSage, LoopSage can be used from any Python script, notebook or console. The package on PyPI is called pyLoopSage; the name to import is loopsage.

pip install pyLoopSage           # add --pre while the release is a release candidate
python -c "import loopsage as ls; print(ls.__version__)"

The Python interface is a set of independent functions, one per step: read the inputs, optimize, run the Monte Carlo, run the molecular dynamics, extract results, draw figures. You call them like any other Python functions and get Python objects back (arrays, tables, figures). Nothing is written to disk unless you pass a folder or call ls.run. The loopsage command and the config file work independently of this interface.

Step Function Returns settings ls.config(...) a Config grid ls.geometry(cfg) region and bead grid inputs ls.read_inputs(cfg, geom, loops=...) InputData Hi-C target (optional) ls.read_hic(cfg, geom, path) (matrix, info) optimizer (optional) ls.optimize(cfg, inputs, geom) and ls.apply_optimum(cfg, result) OptResult, a new Config loop extrusion ls.run_mc(cfg, inputs, geom) MCResult 3D structures ls.run_md(cfg, mc, geom) MDResult results ls.results.<function>(mc, geom) arrays and tables figures ls.plots.<function>(...) matplotlib figures the whole command ls.run(...), ls.main([...]) the run folder is written

docs.title: A first example
docs.text:
import loopsage as ls

cfg = ls.config(region="chr1:77000000-95000000", n_beads=120, n_steps=20000, seed=1)   # all the settings in one Config object
geom = ls.geometry(cfg)                                          # the bead grid: 120 beads of 150 kb
inputs = ls.read_inputs(cfg, geom, loops="loops.bedpe")          # a file path: the loops (BEDPE)

mc = ls.run_mc(cfg, inputs, geom)                                # Monte Carlo loop extrusion

ls.results.mean_loop_length(mc, geom)                            # average loop length (kb) at every snapshot
ls.results.trajectories(mc, geom, "mb")                          # positions of the cohesin legs over time
ls.plots.energy_traces(mc)                                       # a matplotlib figure

Each line is a separate call, so a notebook can run them one at a time, repeat one with other settings, or stop after any of them.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: All settings of a run live in one object, a Config. In Python there is no config file to edit: you create the object with ls.config(...) and pass it to the functions. The same object is used by every step, so the inputs, the optimizer, the Monte Carlo and the molecular dynamics always see the same settings.

docs.title: Create it
docs.text:
Every parameter is a keyword argument, by its key name (n_steps, folding_coeff, run_md). Anything you leave out has its default value.

cfg = ls.config(
    region="chr1:77000000-95000000",     # the genomic region in bp (shortcut for chrom, region_start, region_end)
    n_beads=120,                         # resolution: the region is cut into 120 beads
    n_steps=20000,                       # Monte Carlo steps
    n_lef=8,                             # number of loop extruders
    folding_coeff=1.5,                   # strength of the folding energy
    seed=1,                              # random seed: the same seed gives the same result
)

A command-line option can have a different name than the key: --mc-steps sets n_steps and --md-steps sets sim_step. The tables of the command line and the config file show both names side by side, with the default of every parameter.

docs.title: Read it
docs.text:
Every parameter is an attribute. cfg.source says where each value came from: default for the values you left out, cli for the ones you gave as arguments, and cfg.as_dict() returns everything as a dictionary.

cfg.n_steps                  # 20000
cfg.n_lef                    # 8
cfg.burnin                   # a default value
cfg.source["n_steps"]        # where n_steps came from
cfg.as_dict()                # all parameters as a dictionary

docs.title: Change it
docs.text:
To change settings, make a copy with new values. ls.config(cfg, ...) checks the new values and leaves cfg untouched, which makes it easy to compare settings:

cfg_long = ls.config(cfg, n_steps=100000, seed=2)      # a validated copy with two changes
cfg_nomd = ls.config(cfg, run_md=False)

for f in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0):                              # a parameter scan
    mc = ls.run_mc(ls.config(cfg, folding_coeff=f), inputs, geom)

You can also assign an attribute directly (cfg.n_steps = 5000), but this is not checked: a misspelled name silently creates a new attribute that is ignored, and an invalid value is found only later. Use ls.config(cfg, ...) when in doubt.

docs.title: Find a parameter
docs.text:
ls.parameters("md steps")        # search by name or description: {name: (default, help)}
ls.parameters()["n_steps"][0]    # the default of one parameter: 20000

docs.title: Values and errors
docs.text: Values are converted as in a config file: run_md="yes", integrator_step="100 fs" and bw_files=["a.bw", "b.bw"] all work. A wrong name or an invalid value (for example a burn-in larger than the number of steps) raises ValueError with a clear message, so a script can catch it.

docs.title: From a config file or a dictionary
docs.text:
A config file is optional. If you already have one, ls.config reads it, and your keyword arguments win over its values. A dictionary works the same way.

cfg = ls.config("config.ini", n_steps=5000)                    # the file, with one key overridden
cfg = ls.config({"region": "chr1:1-9000000", "n_beads": 100}, seed=3)     # a dictionary
ls.write_ini("used.ini", cfg.as_dict(), cfg.source)            # save the settings as a config file (optional)

docs.title: The grid
docs.text: ls.geometry(cfg) turns the region and n_beads into the bead grid used by all steps. It has chrom, start, end, n_beads, bp_per_bead and bead_of(bp), which gives the bead that holds a genomic position. Without n_beads, one bead is about 2 kb.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Inputs are given as strings with the path of the file, the same files the command uses:

inputs = ls.read_inputs(
    cfg, geom,
    loops="loops.bedpe",                        # loops: BEDPE with anchors, score and optional CTCF orientation
    compartments="compartments.bw",             # A/B signal: .bw or .bed
    tracks=["h3k27ac.bw", "rad21.bw"],          # extra binding tracks: one path or a list
    lef_track="loading.bw",                     # where LEFs prefer to load
)

Use sites="peaks.narrowPeak" instead of loops for binding sites without loop pairs. Without loops or sites, the config key interaction_file is used, so ls.config("config.ini") followed by ls.read_inputs(cfg, geom) reads the inputs named in the config file.

The result InputData has loops (the profiles L, R, the loop matrix J, cover), BWs (tracks, one row per track), lef_track, comp (compartments in [-1, 1]) and comp_source.

Hi-C reference. ls.read_hic(cfg, geom, "map.hic") returns (matrix, info): the Hi-C map on the bead grid. It is the optimizer target.

Inputs as arrays. For synthetic data, give arrays instead of paths: loops=(left, right, weight) with positions in bp, sites=dict(position=..., weight=..., reverse=...), and per-bead arrays (one value per bead) for tracks, lef_track and compartments. Compartment values must lie between -1 and 1 (A positive, B negative); other values raise ValueError. The sandbox builds such arrays conveniently.

docs.title: Optimizer
docs.text:
The optimizer searches the number of LEFs n_lef, the folding coefficient, the binding coefficient and the temperature by Nelder–Mead, so the simulated map matches a target: the Hi-C map when given, otherwise the loops in inputs.

hic = ls.read_hic(cfg, geom, "map.hic")                         # optional target
result = ls.optimize(cfg, inputs, geom, hic=hic)                # a search of cfg.opt_evals evaluations
result.best                                                     # {'K': ..., 'f': ..., 'b': ..., 'T': ...}
cfg_opt = ls.apply_optimum(cfg, result)                         # a copy of cfg with the optimized values
mc = ls.run_mc(cfg_opt, inputs, geom)
ls.plots.convergence_figure(result)                             # how the search converged

docs.title: Monte Carlo
docs.text:
mc = ls.run_mc(cfg, inputs, geom)
mc.Ms, mc.Ns        # left and right leg (bead number) of every LEF, arrays (LEFs, snapshots)
mc.Es               # energy at every snapshot
mc.chains           # all replicas (cfg.replicas), each with the same fields

A snapshot is saved every mc_step steps; the first burnin steps are the equilibration. The same seed gives the same result.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Functions that turn an MCResult into the quantities one usually needs. geom gives the genomic coordinates. Series cover all snapshots; production=True keeps the snapshots after the burn-in. units is bead, bp, kb or mb.

r = ls.results
left, right = r.trajectories(mc, geom, "mb")        # cohesin legs over time, arrays (LEFs, snapshots)
r.loop_lengths(mc, geom, "kb")                      # loop length of every LEF, (LEFs, snapshots)
r.mean_loop_length(mc, geom, "kb", production=True) # average loop length per snapshot
r.energies(mc)                                      # table: step, total, folding, binding, crossing, temperature, unfolded_fraction
r.loops_table(mc, geom)                             # the loops of the last snapshot as a table (anchors in beads and bp)
r.loop_coverage(mc, geom)                           # average number of loops spanning each bead
r.leg_density(mc, geom)                             # average number of LEF legs on each bead
r.contact_map(mc, geom)                             # contact map implied by the loops, (beads, beads)
r.steps(mc)                                         # Monte Carlo step of every snapshot

docs.title: 3D structures
docs.text:
md = ls.run_md(cfg, mc, geom)                       # OpenMM molecular dynamics from the Monte Carlo loops
md.coords                                           # positions in nm, (frames, beads, 3)

r.coordinates(md, frame=0)                          # one frame, (beads, 3)
r.radius_of_gyration(md)                            # radius of gyration (nm) of every frame
r.distance(md, geom, 80_000_000, 85_000_000, units="bp")   # distance (nm) between two positions in every frame
r.contact_map_md(md)                                # average contact map of the structures, (beads, beads)

The platform, steps and force-field settings are config keys (platform, sim_step, tolerance, ...). Without folder, run_md writes nothing; ls.run_md(cfg, mc, geom, folder="structures_out") also saves the structures and maps there.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
Each figure function of LoopSage is available by name and returns a matplotlib figure (white background) to show or save:

fig = ls.plots.energy_traces(mc)                    # energy and its components over time
fig.savefig("energy.png", dpi=200)

ls.plots.kymograph(mc, geom, inputs)                # LEF positions over time
ls.plots.loop_landscape(mc, geom, inputs)           # loops as arcs
ls.plots.lef_trajectories(mc, geom)                 # tracks of single LEFs
ls.plots.binding_profiles(inputs, geom)             # the binding profiles L and R
ls.plots.loop_matrices(inputs, geom)                # the loop matrices of the inputs
ls.plots.convergence_figure(result)                 # optimizer convergence

All figure functions of the modules in loopsage.viz (mc_figs, map_figs, input_figs, optimizer_figs, structure_figs, ...) can be called this way.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
Functions write nothing by default. To keep results, save what you want: np.save("map.npy", r.contact_map(mc, geom)), r.energies(mc).to_csv("energies.csv"), fig.savefig(...), or mc.save("mc.npz") and md.save("md.npz") for the full result objects (load them again with MCResult.load from loopsage.monte_carlo.simulation and MDResult.load from loopsage.molecular_dynamics.engine).

To write a complete run folder (report, figures, structures, data, exactly like the command), use ls.run:

ctx = ls.run("config.ini", n_steps=20000)            # the pipeline of the command; ctx.dirs.root is the run folder
ctx = ls.run(interaction_file="loops.bedpe", region="chr1:77000000-95000000", out_path="results")

ls.run takes the same arguments as ls.config and returns the run context (ctx.mc, ctx.md, ctx.inputs, ...). Like the command, it saves every output unless it is switched off, for example with report=False or figures=False (the output switches list them all).

docs.title: The command from Python
docs.text:
ls.main(["-c", "config.ini", "-vv"])        # exactly `loopsage -c config.ini -vv`

python -m loopsage -c config.ini does the same from a shell. main takes the list of command-line words; mistakes in the options print the usual usage message and exit.

docs.title: Sensitivity scans
docs.text:
ls.sweep runs a parameter scan on a synthetic polymer and writes the combined sensitivity_report.html, the same as the loopsage-scan command. It returns a result whose .table holds one row per run. See the sensitivity page.

res = ls.sweep({"T": "lin(1, 16, 12)", "n_lef": [4, 12]}, system={"n_beads": 300}, out="my_scan")

docs.title: Importing modules
docs.text:
Every part of LoopSage is importable under the name loopsage, for example import loopsage.monte_carlo as mc or from loopsage.preproc.loader import load_inputs:

Package Contents loopsage.settings the parameters, config files, make_config and load_config loopsage.preproc reading loops, peaks, tracks and .hic files; arrays builds inputs from variables loopsage.motif_finder CTCF motif search and orientation loopsage.monte_carlo energies, moves and the sampler (simulation.run_mc) loopsage.optimizer loss functions and the Nelder–Mead search loopsage.molecular_dynamics OpenMM 3D simulation loopsage.analysis, loopsage.validation maps, features and the comparison with experiment loopsage.knots linking numbers loopsage.viz, loopsage.viz3d, loopsage.reporting figures, the viewer and the report loopsage.pipeline the stages and the runner

The functions above are thin wrappers over these modules, which can be used directly when more control is needed:

from loopsage.settings.loader import make_config
from loopsage.preproc.loader import build_geometry, load_inputs
from loopsage.monte_carlo.simulation import run_mc
from loopsage.analysis.maps import loop_map

cfg = make_config(region="chr1:77000000-95000000", n_beads=120, n_steps=20000, seed=1)
geom = build_geometry(cfg)
inputs = load_inputs(cfg, geom, "loops.bedpe")
mc = run_mc(cfg, inputs, geom, quiet=True)
cmap = loop_map(mc, geom.n_beads)

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text:
The sandbox builds a small artificial system by hand and feeds the same functions. It is useful to test an idea: what does a single CTCF pair do, what do compartments change?

import numpy as np
import loopsage as ls

box = ls.Sandbox("chr1:0-3000000", n_beads=100)          # 3 Mb, 100 beads of 30 kb

# CTCF motifs: position (bp), orientation and strength
box.add_ctcf(300_000, "forward", strength=10)            # forward motif: left anchor of a loop
box.add_ctcf(900_000, "reverse", strength=8)             # reverse motif: right anchor
box.add_ctcfs([1_500_000, 2_400_000], ["forward", "reverse"], [6, 9])      # several at once
box.add_ctcf(2_000_000, 0.3)                             # or a probability of pointing right

# compartments: your own array, one value per bead between -1 (B) and 1 (A)
box.set_compartments(np.sin(np.linspace(0, 12, 100)))
box.add_compartment(0, 500_000, "B")                     # or set a block by hand
# box.random_compartments(mean_block_mb=0.8, seed=1)     # or random alternating blocks

cfg = box.config(n_steps=20000, n_lef=6, seed=2)         # config for this region and resolution
geom = ls.geometry(cfg)
inputs = ls.read_inputs(cfg, geom, **box.arrays())       # the sandbox as inputs
mc = ls.run_mc(cfg, inputs, geom)                        # then everything works as above
ls.plots.kymograph(mc, geom, inputs)
Method What it does add_ctcf(position, orientation, strength) one CTCF motif; orientation is "forward", "reverse", "unknown" or a probability of reverse in [0, 1] add_ctcfs(positions, orientation, strength) several motifs; orientation and strength are one value or one per position add_loop(left, right, weight) a fixed loop between two positions, instead of single motifs set_compartments(values) your array, one value per bead in [-1, 1]; other lengths or ranges raise ValueError add_compartment(start, end, state) A ("A" = 1), B ("B" = -1) or a number in [-1, 1] on a block random_compartments(mean_block_mb, seed) alternating A and B blocks of random length ctcf_sites, compartments the motifs (table) and the signal (array) defined so far config(**parameters) a Config for the region and resolution arrays() the keyword arguments for ls.read_inputs

Use either CTCF motifs or loops in one sandbox, not both.

docs.title: Sensitivity scans
docs.text: loopsage-scan runs many small simulations on a synthetic polymer, varies the parameters you choose, and combines everything into one report, sensitivity_report.html. It answers questions such as: which parameter controls the loop size? where does the system change its behaviour? do links appear in 3D when topoisomerase is slow?

docs.title: Why a sensitivity scan gives biophysical insight
docs.text:
A single simulation shows what one parameter set does. It does not tell you which parameters matter, how strongly, or where the behaviour changes. A scan does, and this is the same thing an experiment does when it varies one condition at a time.

  • Which knob controls which observable. The importance map shows the share of the variance of every output (mean loop size, number of parent and child loops, bound fraction, ...) explained by every input. A knob with a small share can be fixed; a knob with a large share must be measured or fitted.
  • Scaling laws. The elasticity is the percent change of an output per percent change of an input (the log-log slope). An elasticity of 1 means proportional, for example loop size growing with extruder processivity.
  • Interactions. Sobol indices separate the effect of an input alone (S1) from its effect together with others (ST). ST much larger than S1 means the inputs act in combination.
  • Phase transitions and bifurcations. Loop extrusion competes with thermal noise. At low temperature loops freeze, at high temperature they dissolve, and in between the system may change abruptly. A dense scan along one input finds where, and tells a smooth change from a sharp one (see below).
  • Topology. In 3D, loops can link like rings of a chain, and a chain can pass through itself. The scan counts both and shows how they depend on topoisomerase activity and excluded volume.
  • Trust. Every point is repeated with several seeds, so the report shows noise, equilibration and effective sample size next to every result.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
loopsage-scan --init scan.ini      # write a template
loopsage-scan scan.ini --dry-run   # count the runs and estimate the time
loopsage-scan scan.ini             # run; writes results/scan_<name>/sensitivity_report.html

To try it without writing a file, run the demo scan python demo/run_demo.py sensitivity (about 20 s; its settings are in demo/demo_sensitivity.ini).

Open the report in any browser; it is one self-contained file. Finished runs are cached, so re-running a scan after you add a value only simulates the new points, and --replot rebuilds the report without running anything.

docs.title: The scan file
docs.text:
A scan file is an .ini file with five sections.

[scan]                     # how to scan
name       = temperature_and_rings
design     = grid          # grid | oat | random | sobol
replicates = 4             # seeds per point; every point uses the same seeds
snapshots  = 200           # saved configurations per run
metrics    = default       # default | all | a list

[system]                   # the synthetic polymer
n_beads     = 300          # 200 to 500 is typical
bp_per_bead = 10000
n_ctcf      = 12           # CTCF sites
layout      = even         # even | random
orientation = convergent   # convergent | random | forward | reverse

[base]                     # fixed parameters: any key of config.ini
n_steps = 100000

[sweep]                    # what to vary
T     = lin(1, 16, 12)     # 12 temperatures from 1 to 16
n_lef = 4, 12              # two numbers of extruders

Writing an axis. Each line of [sweep] is one input to vary. Values can be a list (4, 8, 16), a range (4:16:4 means 4, 8, 12, 16), lin(a, b, n) for n evenly spaced values, or log(a, b, n) for n values evenly spaced on a logarithmic scale. T is a shortcut that sets both t_init and t_final. Polymer settings are scanned as system.n_beads. Any key of the config page can be an axis.

Choosing a design.

Design Runs Use it to grid product of all axes see every combination, draw heat maps and find transitions oat one axis at a time get a first local picture with few runs random samples quasi-random points cover many inputs with few runs sobol samples x (inputs + 2) measure S1 and ST with confidence intervals

The total is printed first by --dry-run, with a time estimate; max_runs stops accidental explosions.

Defaults of the sandbox. Unless you change them in [base], a scan uses the Metropolis sampler at T = 5 and bind_coeff = 0.05. This is a lively regime for a handful of sites, not a recommendation for real data.

docs.title: Outputs of the report
docs.text:
The report has these sections: Overview, At a glance (plain-language findings and the importance map), Phase transitions and bifurcations, one section per group of outputs (loops, nesting, binding, energy, 3D structure, topology), Quality, Setup and a Glossary. Next to it the scan writes sensitivity_runs.csv (one row per run), sensitivity_points.csv, sensitivity_importance.csv and, for Sobol designs, sensitivity_sobol.csv.

Outputs (metrics) include the mean loop length, unfolded fraction, number of parent loops (hold other loops), child loops (sit inside another), isolated loops, nesting depth, bound fraction at CTCF sites, anchored-loop fraction and energy. loopsage-scan --list-metrics lists all of them.

docs.title: Phase transitions and bifurcations
docs.text:
Give one input at least four values, preferably ten or more, and three or more replicates. The report then follows each output along that input and looks for a sharp change. For every detected change it shows:

  • the order parameter (the output) against the control parameter (the input), with the transition interval shaded;
  • its fluctuations in time (susceptibility), which peak at a continuous transition;
  • the autocorrelation time, which peaks at critical slowing down;
  • a bifurcation diagram: snapshots of the output at each input value, with one line per replicate. Two separate clouds at one value, or replicates that follow different lines, suggest two coexisting states (a first-order transition or a bifurcation);
  • histograms of the output across the transition;
  • with two inputs on a grid, a phase map: the transition line as a function of the second input;
  • if you scan system.n_beads together with system.ctcf_spacing (beads between sites, keeps the density fixed), a Binder cumulant plot whose crossing marks a continuous transition.

The text next to each case states what the numbers suggest and suggests a finer range, for example T = lin(1.8, 4.3, 12), to resolve it. The scan sees only the grid you give it: a steep crossover and a true transition look alike on a coarse grid, and hysteresis (different paths up and down) cannot be tested because each run starts from scratch. Read "possible bistability" as a hint to confirm with more replicates.

docs.title: 3D structure and topology
docs.text:
Add md = true (or --md) to build a short 3D trajectory in every run and report the radius of gyration, compaction, contact-decay exponent and anchor contacts. Add topology = true (or --topology) to also count links between loops and chain crossings:

[scan]
md       = true
topology = true
md_frames = 20             # 3D frames analysed per run

[sweep]
n_lef     = 8, 16
topo_rate = 0.0, 0.01, 0.05   # topoisomerase events

Linked pairs are rare events, so the share of linked loop pairs is pooled over all frames and replicates, with a binomial error bar, rather than averaged run by run. The report also relates crossing leaks (the chain passing through itself even though no topoisomerase acted) to the strand-crossing barrier of the excluded volume. Sweeping a topology setting (topo_*, ev_*) switches 3D and topology on automatically. 3D runs are much slower: use fewer points and check --dry-run.

docs.title: loopsage-scan options
docs.text: Option Meaning scan the scan file -o, --out DIR output folder (default results/scan_<name>) -j, --workers N worker processes (default: all cores; every worker uses one thread) --set SECTION.KEY=VALUE override a setting, e.g. --set scan.replicates=8 --set sweep.T=1,2,4 --md, --topology switch on 3D structures, and link and crossing analysis --dry-run count the runs and estimate the time; run nothing --replot rebuild the report from the cache --no-cache ignore the cache of finished runs --init FILE write a template scan file --list-metrics list all outputs -q, --quiet no progress bar

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
import loopsage as ls

res = ls.sweep({"T": "lin(1, 16, 12)", "n_lef": [4, 12]},
               system={"n_beads": 300, "n_ctcf": 12}, base={"n_steps": 100000},
               replicates=4, out="my_scan")       # writes my_scan/sensitivity_report.html
res.table                                         # one row per run (pandas DataFrame)

res.table has the inputs, the mean of every output over the production part of each run, and, for each output, its autocorrelation time (tau:<name>), its fluctuation (std:<name>) and its Binder cumulant (u4:<name>).

docs.title: Notes on running time and accuracy
docs.text: Runs are independent, so they are spread over all cores, and each run gives up its raw trajectory as soon as the outputs are computed, so memory stays small. The same seeds are used at every point (common random numbers), which makes differences between points much less noisy than the noise of single runs. More snapshots per run do not add independent information; more steps or more replicates do (the Quality section tells you which is needed).

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
Welcome! This part of the documentation explains the ideas behind LoopSage, from the biology of loop extrusion to the physics and statistics that turn it into a working model. You do not need a particular background to read it. Every new word and every symbol is explained when it first appears, so a biologist can follow the mathematics, and a physicist or mathematician can follow the biology.

The pages build on each other, but each one can also be read alone.

  • Scope: what we want the model to explain, and how a handful of simple rules can produce the patterns of a Hi-C contact map.
  • Loop extrusion: the molecular players (cohesin, CTCF, condensin), the loop extrusion model and its assumptions, TADs, loop dots and stripes, and why a snapshot is not enough and dynamics is needed.
  • Mechanics: Hamiltonian, phase space, ensembles and the Boltzmann law, and why an energy-based model is a reasonable approximation for a living cell that is not in equilibrium.
  • MCMC: Markov chains, detailed balance, ergodicity, ergodic means, burn-in and autocorrelation: how the sampler works and how to tell that it worked.
  • Molecular dynamics: the polymer, the force field, Newton's second law and the Langevin equation: how a set of loops becomes a 3D structure.
  • Topology: knots, links and the linking number, how it is computed in 3D, and how LoopSage checks whether loops are interlocked (optional and advanced).

Where to start

If you are new to the field, read the pages in the order above. If you only want to know what a setting does, go to the reference or the implementation pages, which link back here whenever an idea needs more explanation.

docs.title: Loop extrusion
docs.text: This page introduces loop extrusion, the process that folds chromatin into loops. It covers the biology and the basic ideas only. The energy function and the sampling algorithm of LoopSage come in the following pages. The boxes called In LoopSage simply point to the settings where each idea appears in the program.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
A human cell holds about two metres of DNA inside a nucleus only a few micrometres wide. The DNA must therefore be folded, and the folding is far from random: places that are far apart along the DNA are often brought next to each other, which decides which genes can talk to which regulatory elements.

One of the main folding mechanisms is loop extrusion. Picture a ring threaded onto a rope. The ring starts to slide along the rope and pulls the rope through itself, so a loop of rope grows on one side of the ring. In the cell, the ring is a protein complex and the rope is the chromatin fibre.

docs.title: The players
docs.text:
The chromatin fibre is the DNA together with the proteins it is wrapped around. Over distances of thousands of bases it behaves like a long, flexible rope. In all figures it is the black line.

Cohesin is a ring-shaped protein complex that works as a molecular motor. It holds the fibre at two points and, using the energy of ATP, moves these two points apart, pulling more and more fibre through itself. Such a motor is called a loop extrusion factor, or LEF. In the figures, cohesin is the purple ring.

CTCF is a protein that sticks to the DNA at places with a specific sequence, the CTCF motif. The motif has a direction, like a one-way arrow written along the DNA: it can point right (red) or left (blue). CTCF acts as a boundary element, a place where cohesin tends to stop.

Condensin is a close relative of cohesin that works when the cell divides. It is also a ring that extrudes loops, and in the figures it is green. We meet it at the end of this page.

One chromatin loop held by cohesin. The ring encircles the two strands at the base of the loop. The loop is the piece of fibre between the two legs of the ring, at positions mi and ni (ring i). Two CTCF proteins sit at the base, one pointing right (red) and one pointing left (blue).

docs.title: The loop extrusion model
docs.text:
The loop extrusion model (Sanborn et al. 2015, Fudenberg et al. 2016) proposes that a loop is not made by two faraway places that happen to meet. Instead, a cohesin ring sits on the fibre and reels it in from both sides, so the loop keeps growing until something stops the ring.

The life of one loop. 1 A ring holds a short loop. 2 Driven by ATP, its two legs move apart and the loop grows. 3 Two CTCFs that face each other stop the legs. 4 After some time the ring unloads and binds somewhere else, and the old loop is released.

docs.title: How we describe a loop
docs.text:
First we cut the studied region into small, equal pieces called beads (for example 5 000 bases each) and number them \(1, 2, \dots, N_{\mathrm{beads}}\). A bead is simply a position on the fibre, and we write \(k\) for a general bead number.

Usually there are many rings on the region at once, \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) of them, and every ring gets its own index \(i = 1, 2, \dots, N_{\mathrm{lef}}\). A ring has two legs, so ring \(i\) is described by two bead numbers,

\[ (m_i,\, n_i), \qquad m_i < n_i , \]

where \(m_i\) is the position of its left leg and \(n_i\) the position of its right leg. The loop of ring \(i\) is everything between its legs, so its size in beads is

\[ \ell_i = n_i - m_i . \]

The whole system at one moment is then just the list of all pairs,

\[ \{(m_i, n_i)\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{lef}}} , \]

which is \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) pairs of numbers. This short list is all that the stochastic model of the next pages has to keep track of, and every change of the system is a change of one of these numbers.

Symbol Meaning \(N_{\mathrm{beads}}\) number of beads (genomic bins) in the modelled region \(k\) index of a bead, \(k = 1,\dots,N_{\mathrm{beads}}\) \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) number of loop extrusion factors (rings) on the region \(i,\ j\) index of a ring, \(i,j = 1,\dots,N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) \(m_i,\ n_i\) left and right leg of ring \(i\) (bead numbers, \(m_i<n_i\)) \(\ell_i = n_i - m_i\) size of the loop of ring \(i\), in beads \(L(k),\ R(k)\) how strongly a CTCF site at bead \(k\) stops a left leg, respectively a right leg (introduced below)

docs.title: What a LEF does
docs.text:
A ring is always on the fibre, and its life follows a short cycle.

  1. It holds a small loop. A freshly placed ring holds a very short piece of fibre, a loop of one or two beads.
  2. It extrudes. The legs slide along the fibre: the left leg moves left (\(m \to m-1\)) and the right leg moves right (\(n \to n+1\)), so the loop grows. In experiments this happens at about one thousand bases per second (Davidson et al. 2019; Kim et al. 2019).
  3. It stops when a leg meets a barrier: a CTCF with the right orientation, or another ring. The other leg may still move.
  4. It unloads and rebinds. After some time the ring leaves the fibre, the loop is released, and a ring binds again somewhere else. In a living cell the number of rings on the fibre stays roughly constant, so we can think of every ring that leaves as being replaced at once.

The fuel is ATP, the energy currency of the cell. Each step of the ring uses a little ATP, and without it no loops are made (Ganji et al. 2018; Davidson et al. 2019). We do not follow this chemistry in detail. We keep only its result: legs that keep moving outward.

In LoopSage

The number of rings \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) is n_lef, and the number of beads \(N_{\mathrm{beads}}\) is n_beads. A Monte Carlo step either slides the legs of one ring or lets the ring unbind and rebind at a new place, so all n_lef rings are always on the fibre. By default the new place is random; lef_track_file (a cohesin ChIP-seq signal) makes some places more likely.

docs.title: What the model assumes
docs.text:
The picture above rests on a few simple assumptions.

  1. More extrusion than sinking. On average the legs move outward, so loops grow rather than shrink. In the simplest version a leg only moves outward. In a more general version a leg performs a random walk with a drift, so it can also step back from time to time.
  2. Motion is one-dimensional. A leg moves only along the fibre, like a bead on a string. Three-dimensional space matters later, when the loops are folded into a 3D structure.
  3. Rings do not cross. Two cohesin rings cannot pass through each other (see below).
  4. CTCF is a one-way barrier. It stops only a leg that arrives from the correct side (see below).
  5. Rings live longer at barriers. A ring that is stopped by a pair of CTCFs is protected from removal, so it stays much longer than a ring that is just sliding. This is why loops anchored at CTCF dominate experimental data. Typically CTCF stays on DNA for minutes and cohesin for tens of minutes (Hansen et al. 2017).
  6. The data are averages. An experiment measures millions of cells at once, each with its own loops. The model therefore describes a population of possible loop arrangements, not one fixed picture.

In LoopSage

lef_rw = true means that legs perform a random walk; false means that they only extrude outward. lef_speed lets different rings move at different speeds.

docs.title: How CTCF stops cohesin
docs.text:
CTCF stops cohesin in one direction only. A forward CTCF (red) stops a leg that is moving left, head-on towards the arrow tip, and a reverse CTCF (blue) stops a leg that is moving right. So the two CTCFs at the ends of a loop must face each other (this is called a convergent arrangement) to stop both legs.

Four arrangements of two CTCF sites. The pale dashed arc is the loop when the ring starts; the solid arc is the final loop. a Facing each other: both legs stop. b Facing away: nothing stops them. c, d Same direction: one leg stops, the other keeps going. Dots are the legs of the ring, a bar marks a stopped leg, and an arrow marks a leg that is still moving.

This is exactly what data show: loops with CTCF at both ends are mostly convergent (Rao et al. 2014; de Wit et al. 2015; Guo et al. 2015). If the two sites point in the same direction, one leg stays free and keeps extruding, which creates a line of enriched contacts called a stripe. If they face away from each other, no loop is kept.

To use this in a model we only need to state, for every bead \(k\), how strongly it stops a left leg, \(L(k)\), and how strongly it stops a right leg, \(R(k)\). Beads that are not CTCF sites have \(L(k)=R(k)=0\). The direction of each site is read from the DNA sequence of its motif.

In LoopSage

The anchors in the input BEDPE file become the profiles \(L(k)\) and \(R(k)\). If the file has orientation columns (8 and 9) they are used directly; otherwise motif_genome switches on the CTCF motif search (motif_pfm, motif_pvalue), which finds the orientation of every anchor. With data_loss_mode = 1 the barriers are given as a 2D map of loops \((m,n)\) instead of two 1D profiles.

docs.title: Loops, TADs and contact maps
docs.text:
Hi-C is an experiment that counts how often two places of the genome touch each other. Its result is a contact map: a square picture in which the pixel \((i,j)\) is darker when places \(i\) and \(j\) touch more often. Loop extrusion leaves two clear marks on it.

  • Loop dots. The two ends of a stable loop are held together, so they touch more often than expected and form a dark dot, usually at the corner of a square.
  • TADs (topologically associating domains; Dixon et al. 2012, Nora et al. 2012). These are squares along the diagonal. Inside a TAD, rings keep reeling in the whole region, so every place touches every other one. Across a TAD boundary, contacts are rare. A boundary is often a pair of CTCFs facing away from each other, because neither lets rings from the other side come through.

Top: the fibre with loops of cohesin (nested loops inside two TADs) and CTCFs at the domain ends. Bottom: the contact map this arrangement would give. The two squares along the diagonal are TADs, and the dots are loops.

Experiments agree with this picture: when cohesin is removed, loops and TADs disappear, and when CTCF is removed, domains lose their sharp edges (Rao et al. 2017; Nora et al. 2017). In short, cohesin makes the loops and CTCF decides where they stop.

docs.title: Rings do not cross
docs.text:
The fibre passes through the ring, so two rings on the same fibre cannot pass through one another. For two different rings \(i\) and \(j\), with loops \((m_i,n_i)\) and \((m_j,n_j)\), this means that the loops can lie side by side or one inside the other, but they cannot be interleaved and cannot share a leg.

Two cohesin loops. Side by side and nested loops are allowed. Interleaved loops (the legs alternate: mi < mj < ni < nj) and loops that share a leg are not.

As a result, rings push against each other and cannot all collapse into the same loop. They form a chain of neighbouring and nested loops, and the outer legs stay pressed against the next barrier.

In LoopSage

The interleaved case can be switched on or off with cross_loop, and its strictness is set by cross_coeff.

docs.title: Condensin and mitosis
docs.text:
When a cell divides, each chromosome must become a compact rod that can be moved safely into a daughter cell. For this the cell uses condensin (in two forms, I and II). Like cohesin, condensin is an ATP-driven ring that extrudes loops (Ganji et al. 2018), but it differs in three ways.

  1. Longer loops. Condensin makes loops of roughly a hundred thousand to a few hundred thousand bases, arranged in nested arrays along the chromosome (Goloborodko et al. 2016; Gibcus et al. 2018).
  2. No CTCF stops. In mitosis CTCF and most cohesin leave the chromosome arms. The condensin loops are not anchored at fixed motifs, and they form a dense bottle-brush around a central axis. TADs and CTCF loops disappear from the contact map.
  3. They can pass cohesin. Single-molecule experiments show that condensin rings can pass through each other and through other ring complexes (Kim et al. 2020). A cohesin loop and a condensin loop can therefore be interleaved.

a Two cohesins cannot pass each other. b A cohesin (purple) and a condensin (green) can. c In interphase, cohesin loops end at CTCF sites. d In mitosis, condensin loops sit around a central axis and do not depend on CTCF.

In LoopSage

A second group of extruders is added with n_lef2, next to the first group n_lef. Setting between_families_penalty = false lets the two groups pass through each other, while rings of the same group still cannot.

docs.title: Stripes and the need for dynamics
docs.text:
Not every pattern of a Hi-C map is a static picture of one loop. Many maps show stripes: thin lines that start at a CTCF site on the diagonal and run along a row (and, because the map is symmetric, along a column) for tens or hundreds of kilobases. A stripe means that one locus, the stripe anchor, touches many different loci in a row, one after the other.

Loop extrusion explains this naturally if we allow the extrusion to be one-sided (Vian et al. 2018; Barrington et al. 2019). A ring is loaded close to a CTCF site that stops one of its legs. The other leg keeps running, so the loop grows step by step: at time \(t_1\) the loop is short, at \(t_2\) it is longer, at \(t_3\) longer still, until the moving leg is stopped by the opposite CTCF or the ring falls off. At each moment the ring holds one contact, \((m_i, n_i)\), with \(m_i\) fixed and \(n_i\) growing. A Hi-C experiment averages over millions of cells and over time, so these contacts add up to a line.

A stripe is a trajectory. The left leg of a ring rests at a forward CTCF while the right leg moves (pale to dark arcs, times t1 < t2 < t3). Each time point contributes one contact on the row of the fixed anchor, and the average over many rings and times is the stripe on the contact map.

This is an important point for the rest of the documentation. A stable, two-sided loop gives a dot, and a dot can be explained by a single static picture. A stripe cannot: the contact \((m, n)\) changes while the leg moves, and the stripe is the record of this motion. The same holds for the fuzzy "flames" that start at a loop dot, for domains whose inside is enriched, and for the way the strength of a loop depends on how long rings stay on the fibre. All these features make sense only when we know how long a ring stays, how fast it moves and how often it is stopped.

In short, a complete explanation of a Hi-C map needs dynamics, not only the positions of the barriers. This is exactly what motivated LoopSage: a model in which many rings load, extrude, stall and unload on the fibre, so that the contact map is obtained as an average over a simulated trajectory, and the same trajectory can be turned into 3D structures.

In LoopSage

Every leg \(m_i\), \(n_i\) is moved by its own Monte Carlo step: it slides as a random walk or only outwards (lef_rw), with a speed set by lef_speed. A leg that sits on a CTCF site is held there, so one-sided extrusion appears by itself when only one leg is at an anchor. Stripes are never drawn by hand in the Hi-C-like map; they come from the simulated trajectory. See the config reference.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• A LEF (cohesin) sits on the fibre and reels it in from both sides. Ring \(i\) is just a pair of legs \((m_i,n_i)\), its loop has size \(\ell_i=n_i-m_i\), and the whole system is the list of the \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) pairs.
  • CTCF is a one-way barrier: facing sites stop both legs and make stable loops, while sites in the same direction make stripes.
  • Stripes are the record of a leg that moves while the other rests: they need dynamics, not a single snapshot.
  • TADs and loop dots in Hi-C maps are the average footprint of many rings stopped at CTCF boundaries.
  • Cohesin rings do not cross each other, but condensin, which builds the long nested loops of mitotic chromosomes, can pass through cohesin.
