docs.title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
docs.text: The sum \(Z=\sum_x e^{-E(x)/T}\) over all sets of loops is far too large to compute, and so is any average over the Boltzmann distribution. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) avoids the problem. It produces a long random sequence of states whose frequencies approach the Boltzmann probabilities, and then takes averages along the sequence. This page explains why that works and how to tell whether it worked in your run.

docs.title: Stochastic process and Markov chain
docs.text:
A stochastic process is a sequence of random states \(X_0,X_1,X_2,\dots\), one for each time step. In general, each state could depend on the whole past. A Markov chain is a process with a short memory: the next state depends only on the present one,

\[ P(X_{t+1}\mid X_t,X_{t-1},\dots,X_0)=P(X_{t+1}\mid X_t). \]

The chain is described by its transition probabilities \(P_{ij}=P(X_{t+1}=j\mid X_t=i)\). In LoopSage a state is the whole set of loops, and a step is one attempted move (a slide, a rebinding or an epigenetic change). The past matters only through the current loops, which is what makes the chain Markov. The samples are nevertheless correlated, because consecutive states differ by only one move. We return to this in the section on autocorrelation.

docs.title: Which distribution does the chain reach?
docs.text:
A stationary distribution \(\pi\) is one that does not change under a step: if \(X_t\sim\pi\), then \(X_{t+1}\sim\pi\). The initial distribution is the distribution of \(X_0\); in LoopSage it is a random start with loops placed at random. We want a chain whose stationary distribution is the Boltzmann law, \(\pi_i\propto e^{-E_i/T}\), and which forgets its start.

Detailed balance is a convenient way to guarantee the first part. If \(\pi_iP_{ij}=\pi_jP_{ji}\) for every pair of states, then \(\pi\) is stationary. The Metropolis rule achieves this: propose a move to state \(j\) with a symmetric proposal, and accept it with probability

\[ \min\!\big(1,\,\pi_j/\pi_i\big)=\min\!\big(1,\,e^{-\Delta E/T}\big),\qquad \Delta E=E_j-E_i . \]

Moves that lower the energy are always accepted. Moves that raise it are accepted with a probability that falls as \(\Delta E\) grows and rises as \(T\) grows. Only the difference of energies enters, so the partition function \(Z\) is never needed.

Intuition

Think of a hiker who wants to visit places in proportion to how comfortable they are. The hiker always accepts a step downhill, and sometimes accepts a step uphill, more willingly when it is only a small climb or when the weather is warm (high \(T\)). Walking like this for long enough, the time spent at each place matches its Boltzmann probability, even though the hiker never sees the whole map.

a A three-state Markov chain and its transition probabilities. b A chain started in one state approaches the target distribution (dots). c The Metropolis acceptance as a function of \(\Delta E\) for three temperatures.

docs.title: Ergodicity
docs.text:
The second part, forgetting the start, is called ergodicity. A chain is ergodic if it is

  • irreducible: from every state there is a path with non-zero probability to every other state, so no region of states is cut off;
  • aperiodic: it does not return to a state only at multiples of some period \(k>1\).

For such a chain the stationary distribution is unique, and for any start \(P(X_t=i)\to\pi_i\). In LoopSage the moves can reach any arrangement of loops (a ring can unbind and load anywhere), and the chance to stay in the same state keeps the chain aperiodic, so the chain is ergodic in principle.

In principle is not the same as in practice. A chain can be ergodic and still be trapped for a very long time. At low temperature the sampler may stay in one valley of the energy landscape, because leaving it requires a move that the Metropolis rule almost never accepts. This is why LoopSage uses annealing: it starts hot, where barriers are easy to cross, and then cools down so that the chain settles in a deep valley.

a A chain on a connected graph is irreducible; a disconnected one is not. b A chain on a double well mixes at a high temperature and is trapped at a low one. c The running mean reaches the ensemble average only for the mixing chain.

docs.title: Ergodic means
docs.text:
An ergodic mean is the average of a quantity \(x_t=f(X_t)\) along the chain,

\[ \bar x_T=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^{T}x_t \;\longrightarrow\; \langle x\rangle=\sum_i \pi_i f(i)\qquad (T\to\infty). \]

The right-hand side is the ensemble average, the average over the Boltzmann distribution. The ergodic theorem says that the time average along one long ergodic chain equals it. This is what makes the whole method work: we never sum over all states, we simply average over snapshots.

Almost everything LoopSage reports is an ergodic mean over the snapshots after the burn-in: the contact map implied by the loops, the mean loop length, the unfolded fraction, the average of each energy term, the occupancy of each bead by a loop leg, and the insulation or stripe profiles computed from the averaged map. The averaged MD contact map is the same kind of quantity, taken over the 3D frames. These numbers are meaningful when the chain has converged and the number of snapshots is large compared with the correlation time.

What is not an ergodic mean: a single snapshot, the last snapshot, the minimum energy found, and any average that includes the burn-in or the annealing phase (the chain is not stationary there).

docs.title: Reading a run: the burn-in
docs.text:
A chain that starts away from the typical states first drifts, and only later fluctuates around a constant level. The drifting part is called the burn-in, and it is discarded. The mean loop length is a good indicator: at the start the rings are short, then it rises, and in equilibrium it should stay almost constant with fluctuations. A curve that keeps rising or falling is not equilibrated.

Two real LoopSage chains (Metropolis, \(T=1\), 250 beads, 39 extruders, 200 000 steps, one snapshot per 40 steps). a The trace of the mean loop length. b The running mean after the burn-in. c The autocorrelation function. Purple is chain 1 and black is chain 2.

docs.title: Autocorrelation: how long the chain remembers
docs.text:
Consecutive snapshots are similar, so the samples are not independent. The autocorrelation function measures how similar a quantity is to itself after a delay of \(k\) snapshots (the lag),

\[ \rho(k)=\frac{\operatorname{cov}(x_t,\,x_{t+k})}{\operatorname{var}(x_t)},\qquad \rho(0)=1 . \]

How to read it. \(\rho(k)=1\) means that the two values are identical, \(\rho(k)=0\) means that they are unrelated, and a negative value means that they tend to be opposite. A plot of \(\rho\) against \(k\) starts at 1 and decays. The lag at which it reaches about 0 is the time after which the chain has forgotten where it was, so samples further apart than that are practically independent. A curve that stays high for hundreds of lags tells you that the chain moves slowly through the states.

The decay is summarised by the integrated autocorrelation time,

\[ \tau_{\mathrm{int}}=1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho(k), \]

which is the number of snapshots that are worth one independent sample. With \(T\) snapshots, the effective sample size is

\[ \mathrm{ESS}=\frac{T}{\tau_{\mathrm{int}}}, \]

and the error of an ergodic mean is about \(\sigma/\sqrt{\mathrm{ESS}}\), where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the quantity. In the figure above \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\approx240\) and \(740\) snapshots, so each chain of 4750 snapshots after the burn-in is worth only about 20 and 6 independent samples of the mean loop length. This is the honest measure of how much the run really knows.

In practice

Plot the trace: it should fluctuate around a constant after the burn-in. Run two chains from different random starts (replicas): their running means must agree, as in panel b. Read \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\) off the autocorrelation: if it is a large share of the run, increase n_steps, not only the number of snapshots (saving more often adds correlated samples, not new ones). The Monte Carlo page lists the settings, and the report shows the drift of the energy between the two halves of the run.

docs.title: Mechanics of LoopSage
docs.text: LoopSage assigns an energy to every set of loops and samples sets with probability \(\propto e^{-E/T}\). This page explains where that idea comes from, why it is only an approximation for a living cell, and which parts of the exact theory are kept. New words are explained as they appear, so you can read it whether you come from biology, physics, mathematics or computer science.

docs.title: The mechanical Hamiltonian
docs.text:
In classical mechanics a system of \(N\) particles is described by the positions \(q\) and the momenta \(p\) of all particles. Together they form one point \((q,p)\) in the phase space, a space with \(6N\) coordinates (three positions and three momenta per particle). The Hamiltonian \(H(q,p)\) is the total energy as a function of this point: kinetic plus potential energy. For a simple oscillator, for example, \(H=\tfrac12p^2+\tfrac12q^2\). The Hamiltonian determines the motion through Hamilton's equations,

\[ \dot q=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p},\qquad \dot p=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}, \]

where a dot means the derivative with respect to time. As time passes, the system moves along a curve of constant energy.

This requires \(H\) to be differentiable: the force is the derivative of the energy, so a smooth energy landscape gives a well-defined motion. The energy of the loop model is not like that. A loop has integer positions \((m,n)\) on a grid of beads, so there is no derivative, and the loops do not follow equations of motion. Loop extrusion in LoopSage is a statistical model, and for it we keep only a weaker notion of the Hamiltonian, described next.

a A mechanical state is a point in phase space and moves along a curve of constant energy. b An energy landscape turns into probabilities by the Boltzmann law; a higher temperature allows higher energies. c Ensembles differ by what is held fixed.

docs.title: The statistical Hamiltonian
docs.text:
In statistical physics the Hamiltonian can be any function \(E(x)\) that gives the energy of a state \(x\), with no need for derivatives or motion. The probability of a state at temperature \(T\) is then given by the Boltzmann law,

\[ P(x)=\frac{1}{Z}\,e^{-E(x)/T},\qquad Z=\sum_x e^{-E(x)/T}. \]

Here \(Z\) is the partition function, the number that makes all probabilities add up to one. In plain words: low-energy states are likely, and the temperature \(T\) sets how much extra energy is tolerated. In LoopSage, \(T\) is given in arbitrary units, because the energy itself is built from effective terms (folding, binding, crossing) and not from physical joules. A state \(x\) is the complete set of loops \(\{(m_i,n_i)\}\), possibly together with the epigenetic states of the beads.

Intuition

Imagine a marble rolling on hilly ground that is being gently shaken. At low temperature (weak shaking) the marble spends nearly all its time in the deepest valley. At high temperature (strong shaking) it hops between valleys and explores the whole landscape. The Boltzmann law is the exact statement of how much time the marble spends at each height.

docs.title: Ensembles
docs.text:
An ensemble is the set of all possible states together with their probabilities, under given conditions. The three classical ensembles differ in what is held fixed.

Ensemble Fixed Exchanges with the outside microcanonical energy \(E\), particle number \(N\) nothing (isolated) canonical temperature \(T\), particle number \(N\) energy (a heat bath) grand canonical temperature \(T\), chemical potential \(\mu\) energy and particles

LoopSage uses the canonical ensemble: the number of extruders \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) is fixed, and the temperature \(T\) controls the fluctuations. This is why the Boltzmann law above is the right distribution, and why the Metropolis rule on the Monte Carlo page works. The grand canonical alternative, in which extruders appear and disappear, is mimicked by the rebinding move, where one ring is removed and another one is loaded.

docs.title: A cell is not in equilibrium
docs.text:
The Boltzmann law describes a system in equilibrium. A cohesin ring is not in equilibrium: it burns ATP to extrude, and it loads and unloads in a cycle. Such a system is called driven.

What distinguishes equilibrium is detailed balance. Let \(\pi_i\) be the probability of state \(i\), and \(P_{ij}\) the probability to jump from \(i\) to \(j\) in one step. Detailed balance says that for every pair of states the two flows are equal,

\[ \pi_i\,P_{ij}=\pi_j\,P_{ji}. \]

Nothing circulates, and a film of the system looks the same when played backwards. In a driven cycle (load, extrude, release) the forward flow is much larger than the backward flow, so there is a steady current and detailed balance is broken. The system then reaches a steady state: the probabilities \(\pi\) no longer change with time, but they are not Boltzmann probabilities.

a Detailed balance: equal flows for every pair. b A driven cycle has a net current, so it is out of equilibrium. c LoopSage takes the stationary distribution and writes it as an effective energy.

docs.title: The LoopSage approximation
docs.text:
LoopSage does not model the driving. Instead it turns the problem around: whatever the stationary distribution \(\pi\) of the loops is, write it as

\[ \pi(x)\propto e^{-E(x)/T}. \]

The energy is then an effective energy, \(E=-T\ln\pi\) up to a constant. It is not the physical energy of the ring, but a compact way of saying which sets of loops are likely. The terms of \(E\) are chosen to reproduce what is observed: long loops are favoured (folding), legs prefer CTCF sites (binding), and crossing loops are forbidden (crossing). The coefficients are fitted by the optimizer to Hi-C data or to the input loops.

This approximation has a clear limit. Equilibrium sampling gives the right average map and the right fluctuations, provided the effective energy is right, but it does not give the dynamics: the steps of the sampler are not real time, and currents such as the directed motion of a ring are replaced by random-walk moves. Questions about speed, residence times or the order of events need a model with real kinetics.

docs.title: How detailed balance is approximated
docs.text:
The sampler (MCMC) is built so that it satisfies detailed balance with respect to \(e^{-E/T}\) by construction: a proposed move is accepted with the Metropolis probability, which makes \(\pi_iP_{ij}=\pi_jP_{ji}\) for the target distribution. Three design choices keep this approximately true in practice.

  • Symmetric proposals. Sliding by \(\pm1\) is as likely as the reverse move, so the proposal does not bias the result.
  • Rebinding as an approximation. The rebinding move (load a minimal loop anywhere) is not exactly the reverse of the extrusion, so it is a loading process rather than an exactly balanced move. With uniform loading it is close to symmetric. A loading track makes it deliberately biased towards the real loading sites.
  • Annealing. With method = Annealing the temperature changes during the run, so the chain is not stationary until the end. Only the snapshots after the burn-in, when the temperature is close to its final value, are used for statistics.

In LoopSage

The energy terms and the temperature are described in Monte Carlo. The next page explains why the sampler converges to the Boltzmann distribution and how to check that it did.

docs.title: Molecular dynamics of the polymer
docs.text: The Monte Carlo stage gives sets of loops. This page explains the physics that turns them into 3D structures: how chromatin is represented as a polymer, which forces act on it, and how Newton's second law moves it. The settings themselves are on the Molecular Dynamics implementation page.

docs.title: Polymer representation
docs.text:
A chromatin fibre contains billions of atoms. Following all of them is impossible, and also unnecessary. We coarse-grain: a stretch of a few kilobases is replaced by one bead, and only the positions \(\mathbf r_i\) of the beads are followed. Everything finer than a bead is averaged out. The result is a bead-spring chain: neighbouring beads are connected by springs (bonds), and extra terms make the chain stiff and keep beads from overlapping.

a The fibre is replaced by beads. b A bead-spring chain with bonds, angles and excluded volume. c The size \(R\) of a chain of \(N\) beads grows as \(N^ u\); the exponent \( u\) depends on how crowded the chain is.

The size of a chain is measured by its radius of gyration \(R\), the typical distance of the beads from the centre of the chain. It follows a power law in the number of beads, \(R\sim N^{ u}\), and the exponent \( u\) tells how crowded the chain is. An ideal chain that ignores itself has \( u=1/2\), a chain with excluded volume swells to about \( u\approx0.59\), and a compact globule has \( u=1/3\). Chromatin in the nucleus is closer to the compact end, which is why loops and attractive forces matter.

docs.title: The force field
docs.text:
A force field is the list of potential energies \(U\) that define the model. The force on bead \(i\) is \(\mathbf F_i=-\nabla_i U\), which is the slope of the energy landscape pointing downhill: beads are pushed towards lower energy. LoopSage uses the following terms for chromatin.

Bonds keep neighbours at a distance \(r_0\) with a harmonic spring, \(U=\tfrac12k(r-r_0)^2\). The constant \(k\) is large, so the chain is practically inextensible.

Angles give the fibre its stiffness: \(U=\tfrac12k_\theta(\theta-\pi)^2\) is lowest when three neighbouring beads lie on a straight line (\(\theta=\pi\)). A small \(k_\theta\) gives a flexible fibre and a large one a stiff rod.

Excluded volume is a repulsion at short distance. Without it the chain could pass through itself, which a real fibre cannot do. LoopSage uses a soft power law,

\[ U_{\mathrm{ev}}(r)=\left(\frac{\varepsilon^{2}\,s}{r+r_s}\right)^{p}, \]

where \(r\) is the distance between two beads, \(s\) is the strength, \(r_s\) a small softening length, \(\varepsilon\) a fixed constant and \(p\) the exponent that sets how steep the wall is. A softer wall lets strands cross more easily, which is related to what topoisomerases do (see Topology).

Loop springs are the link to the Monte Carlo stage. For every loop of the current snapshot, the two anchor beads are connected by a stiff spring with a short rest length. The anchors therefore sit next to each other, and the fibre between them forms a loop.

Compartment attraction (optional) is a Gaussian well, \(U=-s\,e^{-r^2/2w^2}\), between beads of the same epigenetic state. Chromatin of the same type attracts, so A and B domains separate.

a The harmonic bond and angle potentials. b The excluded-volume wall for three exponents, and the Gaussian well of the compartments. c A loop spring between two anchors.

docs.title: Newton's second law and the Langevin equation
docs.text:
Newton's second law says that mass times acceleration equals the total force. A bead moving in a viscous fluid feels two more forces besides \(-\nabla U\): a friction \(-\gamma m\dot{\mathbf r}\) that slows it down, and random kicks \(\boldsymbol\xi(t)\) from collisions with the surrounding molecules. Together,

\[ m\,\ddot{\mathbf r}=-\nabla U-\gamma m\,\dot{\mathbf r}+\boldsymbol\xi(t). \]

This is the Langevin equation. It is the same picture as a pollen grain in water: the grain is pushed around by countless invisible collisions, and moves in a jittery way. The friction coefficient \(\gamma\) and the strength of the kicks are tied together (the fluctuation–dissipation relation), and together they fix the temperature of the system: they act as a heat bath. The beads then sample positions with probability \(\propto e^{-U/k_BT}\), the same Boltzmann law as on the Mechanics page, now for the shape of the polymer given the loops.

a The forces on one bead. b Time is cut into steps \(\Delta t\). c The mean squared displacement grows as \(t^2\) at short times and as \(t\) at long times.

docs.title: Time stepping
docs.text:
The equation cannot be solved exactly, so time is cut into small steps \(\Delta t\). In each step the forces are computed from the current positions, and the velocities and positions are updated a little. After many steps the chain has moved. The step must be small compared with the fastest motion in the system (the vibration of the stiff bonds and loop springs). Otherwise the numbers grow without bound and the simulation blows up.

Friction makes the dynamics overdamped at long times. This shows in the mean squared displacement of a bead, which grows as \(t^2\) at short times (free flight) and as \(t\) at long times (diffusion).

docs.title: Why MD after Monte Carlo
docs.text: The Monte Carlo stage has no geometry: it only knows which beads are tied together. MD adds the missing physics. The fibre has a thickness, it cannot cross itself, and it has stiffness, so loops compete for space. Between two Monte Carlo snapshots the loops change little, so the chain is not restarted but relaxed from the previous structure for a number of steps with the new springs. The set of frames is the 3D ensemble, and its average is again an ergodic mean (see MCMC).

docs.title: Scope: what the model explains
docs.text: Before the details, let us ask a simple question: what do we want from a model of loop extrusion? This page sets the goal and explains the logic of the approach. The next pages then fill in the physics (Mechanics), the sampling (MCMC) and the 3D polymer (Molecular dynamics). For the biology of cohesin and CTCF, see Loop extrusion.

docs.title: From rules to a heatmap
docs.text:
A Hi-C map is a matrix. Its entry \((i,j)\) counts how often two regions \(i\) and \(j\) of the genome were found close together in space. The map is full of patterns: squares along the diagonal, bright dots at their corners, thin lines called stripes, and a checkerboard. The model asks a generative question: which small set of rules produces these patterns, without drawing any of them by hand?

The rules of loop extrusion are few and easy to state. A ring (cohesin) loads on the chromatin fibre and extrudes a loop. CTCF can stop it. Rings do not cross each other. Because the process is random, a single moment in time shows just one random set of loops. The contact map is the average over many such sets: two regions are often in contact when many of the sets have a loop between them.

a The rules produce random loop states; their average is the contact map. b The patterns that the rules can explain. Compartments are the exception: they need an extra ingredient. Nothing in the map is drawn by hand: the TADs, dots and stripes are what the rules produce.

docs.title: Which patterns can occur
docs.text:
TADs (topologically associating domains) are squares along the diagonal: regions that touch each other more than they touch their surroundings. They appear when loops grow between two boundaries and cannot leave the domain.

Loop dots are single bright points, usually at the corner of a domain. They appear when a ring is stalled at two anchors that face each other (convergent CTCF) and stays there for a long time.

Stripes are lines that start at one anchor. They appear when one leg of the ring is held at an anchor while the other keeps extruding, so that the anchor touches everything along one side.

A/B compartments form a checkerboard: active (A) and inactive (B) chromatin each prefer their own kind. Extrusion alone does not create them, and it even weakens them by mixing regions. They need an attraction between like chromatin, which LoopSage can add with the epigenetic model and the compartment force.

docs.title: The inverse problem: from averages back to cohesins
docs.text: So far we went forward: rules, then loops, then a map. The real situation is the opposite. An experiment gives us only the average, a Hi-C map pooled over millions of cells, and we want to recover what the individual cohesins were doing. This is an inverse problem, and it is the central difficulty of the whole approach.

docs.title: Microstates and averages
docs.text:
Statistical physics separates two levels of description. A microstate is the complete configuration of the system at one moment. For loop extrusion it lists, for every cohesin ring, where its two legs are and how fast each leg moves. A macrostate (or thermodynamic average) is what we can measure without seeing the individual rings: the mean contact map, the average loop length, the average occupancy of an anchor. Writing \(x\) for a microstate and \(O(x)\) for a quantity computed from it, an average is

\[ \langle O\rangle=\sum_x P(x)\,O(x), \]

where \(P(x)\) is the probability of the microstate \(x\). The forward problem gives \(P(x)\) (from a model) and asks for \(\langle O\rangle\). The inverse problem of statistical mechanics gives \(\langle O\rangle\) (from data) and asks for \(P(x)\), or for the energy \(E(x)\) that produces it. In LoopSage the data are the entries of a contact map, a few hundred to a few thousand numbers, while a microstate has several numbers for each of tens or hundreds of rings, and \(P(x)\) has to be given for all of their combinations.

docs.title: Why it is ill posed
docs.text:
A problem is well posed (in the sense of Hadamard) when a solution exists, is unique, and changes only a little when the data change a little. The inverse problem fails these tests in a way that is easy to see.

  • Many microstates give the same average. Averaging throws information away. One ring that stays a long time between two anchors and several rings that visit it briefly give the same contact. Moreover, a map is a static picture, so it cannot tell a fast ring that unbinds often from a slow ring that unbinds rarely if they occupy the sites equally. The speeds of the legs are almost invisible in a steady-state average. The solution is not unique.
  • Small errors in the data become large errors in the answer. A Hi-C map is built from a finite number of read pairs, so it is noisy, especially far from the diagonal. When the map is only weakly sensitive to a parameter, the data cannot pin it down, and a small change of the noise moves the fitted value a lot. The solution is not stable.
  • The data may not be reproducible exactly. A noisy map may be a combination that no model can produce, so we can only ask for the closest solution, not an exact one.

Intuition

Imagine being given only the average arrival time of all trains in a country and being asked for the timetable of each train. Many timetables have the same average. You would need to add assumptions (how trains are scheduled, how many exist) before you could name one.

docs.title: What makes it well posed
docs.text:
The cure is to add information so that exactly one answer remains. Two ingredients are standard.

  1. A known form for the energy. If we fix which quantities the energy depends on, the unknowns shrink from the whole distribution \(P(x)\) to a handful of coefficients \(\lambda_k\). The maximum entropy principle says to take, among all distributions that reproduce the measured averages, the one with the largest entropy, that is, the one that assumes nothing more than the data. It has the form \(P(x)\propto\exp\!\big(-\sum_k\lambda_k O_k(x)\big)\), the Boltzmann law of Mechanics, and with this form the fit has a single solution.
  2. More data than unknowns, and regularisation. Fewer coefficients than independent measurements, together with a mild preference for simple or small coefficients, keeps the answer stable against noise.

docs.title: Our case is harder
docs.text:
LoopSage faces the ill-posed problem without the first ingredient. We do not know the functional form of the energy. Cohesin burns ATP and is out of equilibrium (Mechanics), so there is no reason why a simple Boltzmann energy exists, let alone which terms it has. We therefore propose an effective energy built from a few physically motivated terms (folding, binding, crossing), keep the number of coefficients small, and fit them to data with the optimizer. Two honest consequences follow.

  • A good match between the predicted and the measured map shows that the model is consistent with the data, not that it is the only explanation. Different energy forms could fit equally well.
  • The microstates that the sampler produces are an ensemble that agrees with the average, not a film of what a real ring did. Statements about averages (loop lengths, contact frequencies, stripes) are on solid ground, while statements about the speed or lifetime of a single ring are not.

The way to build trust is to test on information the fit did not use: other chromosome regions, other cell types, orthogonal measurements such as stripes, loop dots or a 3D structure, and to check how much the fitted coefficients change under noise.

docs.title: The two questions
docs.text:
The model has to answer two different questions, and it uses a different tool for each.

  1. Which sets of loops are likely? This is a question about probabilities. It is answered by an energy function together with a Monte Carlo sampler (Mechanics and MCMC).
  2. What does the chromatin look like in 3D when a given set of loops is present? This is a question about motion and shape. It is answered by molecular dynamics of a polymer (Molecular dynamics).

What the model is, and what it is not

LoopSage is a statistical model of loops. It reproduces the distribution of loops and the average structure, but not the movie of one cohesin ring in real time. Its parameters (\(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\), the energy coefficients and the temperature) are effective numbers: they summarise the molecular details, and the optimizer can fit them to data.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text: This page explains the topological side of LoopSage: whether the loops of a 3D structure are interlocked, how this is measured, and which optional switches model it. It is an advanced, optional feature. Nothing here runs by default, and the default model is unchanged.

docs.title: Why look at topology?
docs.text:
A chromatin fibre is a very long thread. In the nucleus a thread cannot pass through another thread, because the two strands repel each other. The only exception is an enzyme called a topoisomerase, which cuts one strand, passes the other through, and seals the cut again. Because of this rule, the way two pieces of fibre are wound around each other is not changed by the usual motion of the chain. It is a conserved property, called its topology.

In loop extrusion this matters in a concrete way. Each ring holds a loop, and the loops of different rings sit close to each other in space. Two loops can lie next to each other like two separate rubber bands, or they can pass through each other like two links of a chain. The second case is called catenation, and it can be created or removed only by strand passage.

docs.title: Knots and links
docs.text:
Topology studies shapes that can be deformed without cutting or gluing (such a deformation is called an isotopy). Two objects count as the same if one can be deformed into the other in this way. A coffee cup and a doughnut are the same in this sense, whereas a doughnut and a sphere are not.

For closed threads there are two basic objects.

  • A knot is one closed curve in 3D space. The simplest closed curve is a round circle, the unknot. A knot proper is a closed curve that cannot be deformed into a circle without cutting it. The simplest example is the trefoil.
  • A link is a set of two or more disjoint closed curves, called its components. The simplest link is the Hopf link: two circles, each passing through the other. The unlink is the trivial case, curves that can simply be pulled apart.

A knot is one closed curve (here the trefoil), a link is several closed curves (here the Hopf link), and in the unlink the curves can be separated. At every crossing, the strand that is cut by a gap passes under the other one.

docs.title: In which dimensions do they exist?
docs.text:
A closed curve is a one-dimensional object. Knots and links need room to go around each other, and the number of dimensions of the space decides how much room there is.

Space What happens a line (1D) a closed curve does not even fit the plane (2D) no knots and no links. Every simple closed curve (one that does not cross itself) is equivalent to a circle (the Jordan curve theorem), and two disjoint circles are either one inside the other or side by side, never interlocked ordinary space (3D) knots and links exist, and there are infinitely many different ones 4D and higher no knots and no links: there is a free direction, so any closed curve can be unknotted and any two curves can be pulled apart

Knots and links are therefore a purely three-dimensional phenomenon. This is why topology cannot be read from the contact map or from the loop list alone, and why LoopSage needs the 3D structures (the molecular dynamics stage) to study it.

docs.title: Knots or links?
docs.text:
For the loops of LoopSage the natural object is a link, for four reasons.

  1. The fibre is not closed. A chromosome piece is an open chain with two free ends, and strictly speaking an open chain cannot be knotted, because a knot needs a closed curve.
  2. Loops are closed curves. The two legs of a ring, \(m_i\) and \(n_i\), are held together by the ring, so they are neighbours in space. The stretch of fibre between them, closed by this short gap, is a closed curve (see below).
  3. The question is about pairs. Loops are short and rarely knot on their own. The biologically interesting question is whether two different loops are interlocked, that is, whether the set of loops forms a link.
  4. The ring itself is a link. A cohesin ring that holds DNA inside it is thought to be topologically linked with it, because the ring entraps the fibre.

Tools that analyse the knots of a single chain, such as the Python package Topoly (Dabrowski-Tumanski et al. 2021), compute polynomial invariants (Alexander, Jones, HOMFLY-PT) of a closed curve. They are the right tool for asking whether a protein or a closed DNA ring is knotted, and they can also compute linking numbers. LoopSage needs one quantity for many pairs of loops in thousands of frames, so it uses its own small implementation of the linking number, defined next, and does not depend on any external topology package.

docs.title: The linking number
docs.text:
The linking number \(\mathrm{Lk}\) is the simplest and most useful number that tells how two closed curves are interlocked. It is defined for two oriented curves, which means that we choose a direction along each curve. Draw the pair on a plane, so that at every crossing one strand is over and the other is under. A crossing between the two curves gets a sign \(\varepsilon=\pm1\):

  • \(\varepsilon=+1\) (right-handed) if the over strand has to be rotated counter-clockwise (by less than half a turn) to point along the under strand,
  • \(\varepsilon=-1\) (left-handed) otherwise.

Then

\[ \mathrm{Lk}(\gamma_1,\gamma_2) \;=\; \frac12 \sum_{\text{crossings between } \gamma_1 \text{ and } \gamma_2} \varepsilon . \]

In plain words, \(\mathrm{Lk}\) counts how many times one curve winds around the other, much as you would count the turns of a rubber band wrapped around a finger.

Crossings of a curve with itself are not counted. Every crossing between the two curves is counted once, and half of the sum is used because, as in the Hopf link, the curves pass each other in pairs.

a The sign of a crossing. b The Hopf link has two crossings of sign +1, so Lk = +1. c Two circles that overlap in the picture but are not interlocked: the same curve is over at both crossings, the signs cancel and Lk = 0. Counting crossings alone would be misleading.

The most important properties are the following.

  • \(\mathrm{Lk}\) is an integer, and it does not depend on how the curves are drawn: any deformation without cutting leaves it unchanged. It is an invariant.
  • If \(\mathrm{Lk}\neq0\) the curves are linked. The reverse is not true: there are linked curves with \(\mathrm{Lk}=0\) (the Whitehead link), so \(\mathrm{Lk}=0\) only says that this simplest test finds no linking.
  • When a strand of one curve is passed through the other curve (which is what a topoisomerase does), \(\mathrm{Lk}\) changes by exactly \(\pm1\).
  • Reversing the direction of one curve changes the sign of \(\mathrm{Lk}\). We therefore report \(|\mathrm{Lk}|\) and call a pair linked if \(|\mathrm{Lk}|\ge 1\).

docs.title: The same number as an integral
docs.text:
The linking number can also be written without any drawing. Let \(\mathbf r_1(s)\) and \(\mathbf r_2(t)\) be points of the two curves. Then

\[ \mathrm{Lk}(\gamma_1,\gamma_2) \;=\; \frac{1}{4\pi}\oint_{\gamma_1}\oint_{\gamma_2} \frac{(\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2)\cdot(\mathrm d\mathbf r_1\times \mathrm d\mathbf r_2)}{\lVert \mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2\rVert^{3}} . \]

This is the Gauss integral (Gauss, 1833), and its meaning is geometric. The unit vector \((\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2)/\lVert\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2\rVert\), which points from one curve to the other, changes as the two points move along their curves, and it covers the sphere of directions a whole number of times. The factor \(1/4\pi\) is the inverse of the area of the unit sphere, so \(\mathrm{Lk}\) is exactly how many times the sphere is covered.

docs.title: Why is it hard to compute in 3D?
docs.text:
The drawing recipe needs a projection of the 3D curves onto a plane. For a computer model, which is a chain of beads joined by straight segments, this causes several problems.

  1. The picture depends on the viewing direction. From one direction the two loops cross twice, from another four times. Only the signed sum is the same.
  2. Some directions are bad. If we look along a direction in which two segments overlap, or a bead lies exactly behind another segment, the crossing is degenerate and the over/under decision is not defined. One has to find a "generic" direction, or average over many.
  3. Structures are noisy. A molecular dynamics frame is a wiggling polymer with segments that pass very close to each other. A tiny change of the viewing direction can create or remove crossings.
  4. Closed curves are needed. The loops of a chain are open pieces of the fibre.
  5. There are many pairs and many frames. A region has tens of loops, so hundreds of pairs, in every analysed frame.

One pair of linked loops, taken from a 3D polymer, seen from three directions. The number of crossings changes (2, 4, and an almost edge-on view in which the crossings pile up), but half the sum of the signs is always +1, which was also computed with the Gauss integral. The pictures are generated from the actual 3D coordinates.

docs.title: What LoopSage does
docs.text:
LoopSage avoids projections completely and computes the Gauss integral directly on the 3D coordinates.

  1. Closing the loops. Every loop is the piece of the chain between the two legs of a ring, beads \(m_i,\dots,n_i\). The closing segment between the two anchors (the chord) turns it into a closed polygon. This is a good approximation because the ring holds the two anchors next to each other.
  2. Choosing the pairs. Only pairs of loops that are really two separate curves are tested. Nested or overlapping loops share a piece of the chain, so they are not two separate curves and are skipped, and a loop of fewer than 4 beads is too short to count as a curve. What remains are loops that lie side by side along the chain, which can still be interlocked in 3D.
  3. An exact formula for polygons. For two closed polygons the double integral becomes a finite sum over pairs of segments, one term for every segment of the first loop and every segment of the second (Klenin and Langowski 2000). Each term is the signed area on the unit sphere swept by the direction between the two segments, written with the four unit vectors that join their end points. The sum divided by \(4\pi\) is an integer up to rounding errors, and LoopSage rounds it to obtain \(\mathrm{Lk}\). The result is exact for the polygon, needs no projection and has no degenerate directions.
  4. A cheap pre-filter. Two curves whose bounding boxes do not overlap cannot be linked, so the sum is computed only for pairs whose boxes overlap.

a A loop becomes a closed curve when its two anchors are joined by a chord. b Only pairs of loops that are separate curves are tested. Nested or overlapping loops and loops shorter than 4 beads are skipped.

docs.title: Linking in LoopSage
docs.text:
In LoopSage

The linking analysis is switched on with --knots (key detect_knots) and works on the 3D structures, so it needs the molecular dynamics stage (run_MD = True). The name knots is historical: the quantity that is computed is the linking number of pairs of loops, as explained above.

For every knots_stride-th MD frame, LoopSage takes the loops \((m_i,n_i)\) of the Monte Carlo configuration that belongs to that frame, closes them, tests all admissible pairs and stores the pairs with \(|\mathrm{Lk}|\ge1\). From this it reports:

  • the number of linked pairs per frame, next to the number of pairs that were tested,
  • the lifetime of a link, which is the number of consecutive analysed frames in which the same pair stays linked, and how many links are formed and dissolved at each step,
  • the closest approach of two loops, and a link map, which shows where along the chromosome linked pairs occur,
  • 3D snapshots of linked examples, in which the two loops are drawn thick and closed by their chords, and a gold marker shows where they meet.

docs.title: Why links appear and disappear
docs.text: If the excluded volume were perfect, strands could never cross, and the topology of the chain could not change during the molecular dynamics. Links would then come and go only because the loops themselves change: the Monte Carlo trajectory moves the legs, so the pairs of loops that are analysed are not the same in every frame. The second source of change is the topoisomerase.

docs.title: The topoisomerase and the crossing counter
docs.text:
LoopSage offers two optional models of a topoisomerase II. Both are set in the [topology] section and both are off by default.

  • random mode (ev_p, continuous_top). In every frame a random fraction ev_p of the beads has its excluded volume switched off, either scattered or as one continuous stretch (continuous_top). Strands can pass through these beads.
  • local mode (topo_mode = local). Short strand-passage events: at close contacts, a strand of topo_width beads loses its excluded volume for a short window topo_window of the frame, and then the volume is switched on again. The attempts occur at a rate topo_rate per frame and per 1000 beads, between strands closer than topo_radius bond lengths. With topo_keep < 1, a passage that creates a new link is undone with probability \(1-\)topo_keep, which models a topoisomerase that simplifies the topology.

a Random mode: in every frame some beads have no excluded volume (dashed), scattered or in one stretch, and a strand can pass through them. b Local mode: two strands come close, a short stretch of one loses its excluded volume for a short window, the other strand passes through, and the volume is restored. A passage that creates a new link can be undone.

The crossing counter (track_crossings, checked every track_every MD steps) detects two bonds that pass through each other between two checks. Crossings that occur with the excluded volume on are leaks of the force field, and crossings through a switched-off bead are passages.

How easily strands cross is controlled by the excluded volume \(E(r)=\big(\varepsilon^2 s/(r+r_0)\big)^{p}\), where \(s\) is the strength (ev_ff_strength), \(p\) the exponent (ev_ff_power), \(r\) the distance between two beads and \(r_0\) a small softening length. Two bonds can cross only if four bead pairs overlap, so the barrier for a crossing is the lowest value of the sum of \(E\) over these four pairs, in units of \(k_BT\). A barrier of a few \(k_BT\) is crossed easily, while about \(10\,k_BT\) or more keeps the chain intact. The topology report prints the barrier of the current setting, and ev_barrier_target is the barrier for which it suggests a new ev_ff_strength.

docs.text:
Key Meaning detect_knots (--knots) linking analysis of the loops in 3D knots_stride analyse every n-th MD frame topo_mode random (default) or local topoisomerase model ev_p, continuous_top random mode: share of beads without excluded volume, and whether they form one stretch topo_rate, topo_radius, topo_width, topo_window local mode: rate, reach, strand length and duration of the passage events topo_keep local mode: probability to keep a passage that creates a link (1 = no bias) track_crossings, track_every count chain crossings, and how often to check ev_barrier_target barrier (in \(k_BT\)) used to suggest ev_ff_strength

All keys are described in the config reference, and examples/11_topology_links.ini is a ready-made example.
